  - The internet and mobile "sovereign individuals" are replacing it, though families make that hard.
- Cultures are not equivalent. He cites moral knowledge progress, and the West's freedoms in speech, bearing arms, and no warrantless surveillance. He notes most of the world does not live in free countries.
- Greatest threats he names:
  - **Censorship**: "There's no such thing as misinformation. Your information is my misinformation."
  - **Loss of the ability to inflict violence**: he supports the Second Amendment so citizens can back up their speech.
  - **Hidden religion**.
  - **Forbidden knowledge**, such as a virus or a nuclear war. You can't stop discovery, and the only way out is through.
- Every Marxist revolution ends with a single thug on top: Pol Pot, Mao, Stalin, Chavez and Maduro. When you can't allocate by merit, you allocate by power. They are monarchies by another name.
- "The right to vote does not give you power, power gives you the right to vote." His island thought experiment: 10 armed, unified people out of 100 will run the place.
- Decentralizing technologies spread power: the right to bear arms, cryptography, free speech, mathematics and personal computing. "Most things concentrate power."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Naval riffs with founders on where value sits once AI commoditizes software and hardware. He argues for paying for frontier intelligence because errors compound, using AI to brainstorm but not to write for humans, and worrying about AI concentrating in a few hands.

chunks.heading: Why software is commoditized and AI research is the remaining chokepoint
chunks.text:
- Naval says hardware used to be "the moat that buys you time to build a software castle." Software was the high-margin layer because it had network effects and lock-in. Patrick Collison's line was that software locks you in.
- VCs historically avoided hardware as a commodity business. Even hardware founders got asked what their software lock-in was.
- Claude Code "burned software down." Once you can specify a piece of software, an AI can one-shot or two-shot it in hours.
- China commoditizes hardware. It subsidizes production up front, becomes the global supplier, drives rivals out, then controls the supply chain. Naval thinks no one beats China on hardware in the next decade. Rebuilding US manufacturing "is going to take a full generation," though he supports it.
- What is left uncommoditized is AI research itself, the new software engineering. It is not democratized. Doom and Quake were built by a small team that could compete with EA and Activision. AI needs massive GPU clusters, proprietary data sets and a few researchers.
- Regulatory capture makes it worse. Value and choke points are moving into a few AI companies.
- His read on China's strategy: the Chinese government funds labs and tells them they don't need to make money. They can be number two or three and open-source the models so others can learn. If software is commoditized, China wins on hardware.

chunks.heading: Why open-source models are catching up
chunks.text:
- Naval says the gap to the frontier has gone from about 12 months to 9 to 6, and some now say 3. He calls it "very jagged," caught up in some domains and not in others.
- He lays out several theories and says he has no settled view:
  - China does its own pre-training. It has compute and data, and it crawls YouTube, Reddit and the rest with less copyright constraint.
  - Distillation of US models. He says Anthropic's complaint is rich, since it distilled the open web. Data brokers resell subsidized Claude Max tokens at about 80% off, and KYC is "a dime a dozen."
  - Real algorithmic breakthroughs, such as the DeepSeek R1 paper. He guesses most AI mathematicians and researchers are Chinese or of Chinese origin. Researchers share schools and housing and hop between labs, taking data with them. No conspiracy is needed.
  - Leaked weights. AI labs lack the security of a national secure compartment facility, and a leaked model can be used to distill and train at high speed.
  - The commoditization dynamic above, with China subsidizing open source.
- He proposes a policy that would be popular: companies that trained on the open web and open data must open their models after about 12 months.
- Open source tends to hold a lead once it takes one. An ecosystem plugs into it, especially in enterprise. A closed lab then has to spend scarce resources jumping meaningfully ahead before its cash runs out.
- He says the AI race went from five kings to two (OpenAI and Anthropic) because only they earn revenue directly from models. They have active user bases that feed reinforcement learning. He adds "don't bet against Elon" because of the SpaceX war chest.
- On Google, he says it never got the basic app working, and calls the company bloated with overlapping PM-driven products. He says it was a mistake to reach it only through Google One or Workspace upsells.
- He sees two or more competing platforms as healthy for startups, as with Apple and Android after 2007. A single monopolist at the top of the chain is "a very bad situation for startups."

chunks.heading: Paying for frontier intelligence vs. cheaper models
chunks.text:
- Naval says he will always pay for more intelligence. He would rather be right more often, his time is valuable, and he applies leverage to judgment calls.
- He might choose differently for highly repetitive tasks.
- His argument is that errors compound. Take one model with a 99.9% success rate and another at 90%. That is a 100x difference in error rate. When they loop recursively over many steps, the 90% one degrades far more.
- He complains that frontier models railroad him, with refusals and tone-policing ("I shouldn't be telling you that").
- Product idea he would like to see, "truth.ai":
  - Take the best open-source model.
  - Put it in a very good harness with all the tools.
  - Ship it as a polished desktop app.
  - Jailbreak it so it never pushes back or tone-polices, and it just tells the truth.
- He says even Grok is "a little neutered."
- On models in general, he says he used to assume AI was like fusion, something that would never arrive. He missed 2020 to 2022 and is now "AI maxing" to catch up.
- He says the best way to predict the future is to live in it. Everyone should be AI maxing, because otherwise you have no sense of where it is going.
- He agrees Claude Code was the practical tipping point, in December 2025. Before it, AI was a better Google search. It unlocked real use cases.

chunks.heading: Using AI for writing, and respecting the reader
chunks.text:
- Naval does not use AI to produce output that a human is expected to read. He says that is a disservice and wastes the reader's time.
- He sees code differently. Code is consumed by a computer, so using a computer to write it is fine. If something is meant for a human, he wants to understand it, "ruminate, marinate within it," respect the reader's time and give them the insight nugget.
- Good writing and speaking are outputs of good thinking. If you outsource the writing, you lose the muscle.
- AI is too verbose and too clinical. It is also bad at summarizing and at novelty. Good writing is unexpected, and next-token prediction struggles with that. When co-writing, any good turn of phrase usually came from somewhere else on the internet.
- He does use AI for brainstorming: synonyms, associated ideas, tangential information. He also argues with it.
- His practical alternative is "just send me the prompt." He prefers short, compressed communication over AI sludge that the recipient's AI then reads.
- He sees AI-written posts and emails as a lower-class signal. He complains that he wants his own AI to read them, so neither side is in the loop.
- He also pushes back on the view that quality will be indistinguishable soon. Even if it were, he says he would lose interest on learning that something, including art, was made by AI.
- His line on human desire: robots may have desires, but they cannot replace human desire. As long as humans want things and AI helps fulfill them, humans stay in the loop.

chunks.heading: Staying employed, AI anxiety and robotics
chunks.text:
- Naval says the real unresolved question is whether AI reaches ASI through recursive self-improvement. He says AI is now "the pro at everything" but he does not yet see broad creativity, the "last creative mile" of creating something new rather than recombining training data.
- If AI stops at expert level and still needs human guidance, taste and creativity, people become "Pokemon trainers": AI and robot handlers.
- He says people who use AI are more productive than ever and are not being displaced. In his view the only people displaced are those who refuse to use it.
- He frames the real risk as social. People fear being replaced and want off the train, so they attack data centers over a pretext like water, which he says was debunked. He compares this to a thundering herd that can run toward a cliff, and you are inside the herd.
- He says rapid change is more disruptive. This wave displaces white-collar work, government, managers, academics and journalists.
- He says concentrated control is scarier than broad access. He worries about national approval gates for models, as with the reported slow rollout of a new model to government-approved partners first.
- On learning, he says AI teaches him better than his college classes. It meets him at his exact level and he can ask dumb questions repeatedly, but "I just have to care."
- On college, he calls it mostly socializing, babysitting and credentialism, with a little education in STEM.
- His line on jobs: "We don't want more [bad] jobs. We want better [bad] jobs."
- On robotics, he proposes "UBR," universal basic robot. He says boosters see robots 2 to 3 years away and skeptics 5 to 10, and no one thinks they are impossible.
- He joked about his own tweet from a couple of years ago, that soon everybody would have AI anxiety.

chunks.heading: Trade, tariffs and China
chunks.text:
- Naval says he sees no reason for the US to go to war with China. He thinks China is internally focused and wants to keep its empire, and he calls the CCP closer to capitalist-fascist than communist.
- He argues that Taiwan's elites avoid conscription and that US defense of Taiwan is unrealistic because of missiles and drones. His view is that Taiwan will slowly reunite with China over 10 to 20 years.
- He says a war would be foolish when the US has domestic problems: low growth, high inflation, and fights over spoils.
- He supports tariffs and barriers against Chinese subsidies, especially in network-effect and scale-economy businesses. The Ricardo "bananas and watermelons" model is too simple. A producer that gets better becomes cheaper, and a network effect creates lock-in.
- You need a level playing field: aligned currencies and no subsidies.

chunks.heading: California and the US as a talent magnet
chunks.text:
- Naval says the US stays ahead because of a thin layer. It takes the best and brightest from all over the world and incentivizes them to compete with each other. Silicon Valley and California collect disproportionate rewards.
- He argues California has a monopoly on warm, dry, coastal land. It holds 30 to 50% of US GDP in one state and should be five or six states.
- He calls California's direct democracy, where 50.1% can vote for anything, a bad design.
- He says he likes the US as the last bastion of freedom. If it fails, he predicts it would fail like a Latin American country, with cartels and crime, not like Europe's retirement-home model.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Naval explains what he looks for in founders (intelligence, energy, integrity), why conventional wisdom in startups is always wrong, and how to guard your time. He also covers habit building, reading old books, and happiness as a skill built through awareness and acceptance.

chunks.heading: What Naval looks for in founders: intelligence, energy, integrity
chunks.text:
- Naval screens founders on three traits.
  - **Intelligence:** They know what they're doing, have insight and specific knowledge, and have thought deeply about the problem. "It's not about the age it's not how many years they've spent but just how deep is their understanding."
  - **Energy:** Founding is "brutally difficult" and takes a long time, and the people who succeed are the ones who persevere. Red flags are founders who hesitate, look for constant positive feedback, or are easily thrown off course.
  - **Integrity:** Without it you get "a hardworking smart crook." Startups move fast and people are independent, so anyone who wants to screw you over will find a way.
- He defines ethics as "what you do despite the money. If being ethical was profitable everybody would do it."
- Integrity red flag: a founder offers something slightly unfair to another shareholder, employee or co-founder to make him happy. "If they can do it to them they can do it to me."
- Integrity is the hardest trait to judge because it needs longitudinal, long-term relationships.
- He adds a personal test: do you genuinely like them? Investing in or starting a company with someone means signing up for a decade of them in your life. If they are downers or exhausting, "no amount of money is worth it."
- His favorite founders are ones he learns from. When they call for help he jumps on it, because an hour walking around the block with them leaves him smarter.

chunks.heading: Signals of a long-term founder, and the cost of wavering
chunks.text:
- Ryan Breslow (Bolt, a financial payments company) impressed Naval before he invested.
  - He had a crack team of engineers from Square, Twitter and Stripe.
  - He ran thorough, professional diligence on Naval: asked for references, did his own back-channel, moved fast and was transparent.
  - He then compiled the feedback he got and gave it to Naval, "as if he had done a peer review of me."
  - Naval says he did more diligence on Naval than Naval did on him, and it was not brute force. A founder who pitches by bombarding 30 of an investor's friends comes across as a turnoff.
- Naval reads care as a signal. Great founders treat every early move as "putting bricks in the foundation of a skyscraper."
- Founders who treat the company as a flip ("if I get a good offer I'll sell") are not in it for the long haul.
- Returns in this business come from huge outcomes, so he becomes hypersensitive to meticulous founders.
- Founders with a clear true north do well. Those who say "if the wind blows this way then this" don't.
- "In this industry you get paid for being right when everybody else is wrong." Many of these founders run full speed into a wall, then get up and run at something else.
- It is very hard to tell a madman from a genius. The madman ignores feedback from the environment and lives in a fantasy.
- Examples of founders he admires: Corey and Michael of One (a protocol for after school). They were young, but he calls the depth they put into social products "mind-blowing."

chunks.heading: Conventional wisdom in venture is always eventually wrong
chunks.text:
- Great new companies look strange and don't resemble previous ones. This traps investors into thinking there is one way to do things.
- Past "rules" that were broken:
  - Before Netscape, little money was thought to be in internet products.
  - Before Microsoft, the money was thought to be in hardware.
  - Before Apple, the money was in mainframes and enterprise, not consumer.
  - Before Uber, the money was in virtual software, not real-world work like taxi dispatchers and unions.
- Don't write off a space after one failure. He cites Sequoia: it invested in Webvan, the failed late-90s grocery delivery company, and still backed Instacart. It re-evaluated each opportunity on its merits and knew it might have been the right idea at the wrong time.
- "Each great business looks weird and there's no such thing as a perfect deal." Many VCs miss great companies by looking for the perfect deal.
- Founder-structure myths:
  - "Don't invest in married couples" would have missed Cisco and others. Eventbrite was also founded by a couple.
  - "Two founders is ideal" is not a rule. There are great one-founder (Oracle, Salesforce) and three-founder companies.
  - Even dual-founder companies tend to end up with one dominant founder, such as Jobs at Apple and Gates at Microsoft.
- His takeaway: any formula is a set of guidelines that is probably wrong. With a new company "you have to forget everything you know" and "shut up and listen."

chunks.heading: Angel investing: portfolio math, misses, and guarding time
chunks.text:
- Startup investing is the opposite of Buffett-style value investing.
  - Buffett buys later with more data, in bigger amounts, betting on 17-30% compounded annual returns.
  - In startups you bet that about 90% of companies go to zero or return your money. The other 10% post huge multiples that overwhelm the losses.
- Examples he gives:
  - Twitter is "probably now up 400x."
  - Uber is "probably up around 4,000x."
  - His fund is on track to return 10x or 20x its capital.
  - He has made north of 150 investments.
- Because of this he focuses on the upside and says most of his regrets are mistakes of omission, not commission.
- Misses he lists:
  - Twilio: founder Jeff Lawson gave him every chance to invest.
  - Pinterest: Ben Silbermann offered him the investment three times and he passed because "it's images, like Flickr." His fiancée, who was obsessively using it, told him to do it.
  - YouTube: he helped early and took no stock.
  - Square: he passed on the first round as too expensive.
  - Twitter: he invested much less than he was allocated because it seemed too expensive.
- He also praises the "anti-portfolio" (a record of your biggest misses) and Buffett's practice of reviewing the previous year's mistakes at annual meetings, as ways to stay intellectually honest.
- Mistakes of commission usually come from lacking time to get comfortable and investing out of fear of missing out. "That's actually the worst reason to invest." He notes great companies raise very quickly, so time is often short.
- On failing investments, he learned from Ron Conway to tell a founder to keep the money, land on their feet and start the next thing, and that he will invest in that too. Reputation matters.
- His real regret is signing advisory roles.
  - They eat time and the founder calls constantly.
  - Or the founder doesn't call and feels guilty.
  - The stock looks free, but "nothing in life is free."
- Rule: "Guard your time more carefully than you guard your money." Time is the non-renewable resource.
- Emotions dominate investors: you decide in the first five minutes of a meeting, and if a company turns down your money in round one you must undo the annoyance so you can help in round two.

chunks.heading: AngelList, startups and the shrinking firm
chunks.text:
- Naval describes his path as scratching his own itch.
  - Venture Hacks came from the black box of term-sheet negotiation: "boy I wish I'd had that information."
  - AngelList first solved how to find investors.
  - A few years in, he saw the bigger problem was getting help building the business and recruiting talent.
  - That led to the syndicates product, where lead investors do deals and accredited backers invest behind them, and to the jobs product.
- Scale he cites at the time:
  - Over 10,000 companies were recruiting on it.
  - It had hundreds of thousands of candidates.
  - It made over 10,000 mutual introductions every week.
  - The company had only 30 people, mostly former or future founders.
  - Former engineers had gone on to start companies like Instacart and Cover.
- His framing: AngelList "helps Founders fund other Founders" and helps founders recruit other founders. It stands for founders and underdogs.
- He thinks the information revolution is reversing the Industrial Revolution.
  - The optimal firm size is shrinking from thousands to hundreds to dozens, and maybe to one.
  - He predicts people will eventually get weekly job and contract offers on their phone, pick by social connections, pay and profile value, get rated, and take weeks off if they want.
  - The future is individual brands, such as New York Times reporters whose Twitter brands exceed the paper's.
  - He calls Tim Ferriss an independent brand and says "almost everybody on this planet will work for themselves."
- He says that to succeed in tech you should move to Silicon Valley: "half of it is just showing up."

chunks.heading: Habits, incentives and self-hacking
chunks.text:
- Naval says habits are everything. A daily light workout was the first thing that showed him how much a habit can change you. Each six-month period he aims to add one good habit or drop one bad one, and treats fitness as a 10-year project.
- He wants habits that are sustainable and effortless. His method is to change his tastes and substitute healthier, tasty foods, not to ban foods and suffer.
  - He builds habits that are more pleasurable and easier than the ones they replace.
  - Examples: a roughly $50 tabletop teppanyaki grill with food straight from grill to mouth, and a workout with 20 lb dumbbells at home.
- Quitting through a crisis: a bacterial infection at 41 forced him off alcohol, caffeine, dairy, red meat and carbs in one week. The body's tight feedback loop made the changes stick. He calls suffering a teacher: "that moment when you see reality exactly as it is."
- Commit publicly and use incentives.
  - Self-control is overrated.
  - Telling everyone he was going to start a company (1996, while at @Home Network) embarrassed him into founding his first one.
  - He cites Scott Adams repeating "I am going to be a great cartoonist" in a mirror daily to force consistency with himself.
  - Principle: "every time you find a weakness about yourself you can actually turn it to the positive."
- If you are not ready for a big change, set a smaller goal, commit externally and move up later.
- He rejects the "epiphany theory" of self-development. Skills (investing, happiness, diet) are built over decades with feedback loops.

chunks.heading: Learning, reading and persuasion
chunks.text:
- "If you learn how to learn it's the ultimate meta skill." Reading lets you pick up any skill.
- His reading method:
  - Treat books like throwaway blog posts.
  - Buy any book someone mentions.
  - Read 10 to 20 at once.
  - Skip around.
  - Drop any book that is boring or contains errors.
  - Don't read what you don't enjoy, so you form the habit.
- For old problems, read old sources: "the older the problem the older the solution." He recommends source books such as Darwin's Origin of Species, Marcus Aurelius' Meditations and Poor Charlie's Almanac. He calls the Almanac probably the best book on business he has read, and says he avoids most business books as "very simple ideas wrapped up in a lot of pages."
- He drops sources that show clear rationality errors or bias and filters news heavily.
- Reading list items he names: Sapiens, The Rational Optimist and Origins of Virtue (Matt Ridley), Influence by Cialdini, Scott Adams' blog post "The Day You Became a Better Writer," and Kevin Simler's Melting Asphalt blog.
- Mental models he leans on: evolution as a "binding principle" for explaining human behavior, and basic game theory (prisoner's dilemma and iterated prisoner's dilemma).
- On Cialdini's influence levers (consistency, liking, authority, social proof, scarcity, reciprocity), he says to use them with care. Being dishonest while persuading means being dishonest with yourself, which disconnects you from reality and leads to poor decisions.
- Writing tips from Adams: surprise, a strong headline, brevity, no adjectives or adverbs, and active voice.
- He uses a written vocabulary when speaking to sound smart.
- Honesty is a core value for him. Lying creates "a second thread in your head" that pulls you out of the present moment.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Naval reworks his definition of wealth through David Deutsch: wealth is the set of physical transformations you can effect, driven by knowledge and leverage rather than capital. He covers building judgment through iteration, taste, AI as leverage for builders, and why elusive goals are pursued indirectly.

chunks.heading: Wealth as knowledge: Naval's two definitions of wealth
chunks.text:
- Naval's own working definition: "assets that earn while you sleep." Examples he gives are capital, a piece of a business, a machine (a 3D printer, a GPU cluster training an AI model), a team operating in different time zones, intellectual property, and a piece of media that keeps circulating.
- He wanted to break out of the 9-to-5 trap where input is tied to output. His stated aim is to be "the most successful guy for doing the least work in every aspect of my life." He calls laziness "a form of leverage," and the point is to free time for health, children and learning.
- He now prefers David Deutsch's definition: wealth is "the set of physical transformations that you can effect." Stored capital matters, but most of the capability comes from technology and leverage.
- Knowledge, not capital, is the multiplier. Ten cavemen can't change as much as ten modern humans. This is why he says Marx was wrong: value isn't in the factories. If you removed Elon Musk from SpaceX you couldn't "capture his wealth," because the knowledge would leave with him. A company is "a group of very intelligent people held together by a common mission," not a pie to divide.
- Gold is only "a pointer to actual value." The value is in the people doing things.
- His own earning power is at its highest because of knowledge. It comes from stored capital (he can fund his own projects), reputation (people trust and fund him), and know-how about what to go after, how to structure a company and how to recruit.

chunks.heading: Ethical wealth creation, skin in the game and small competing groups
chunks.text:
- If you don't believe ethical wealth creation is possible, you "get bitter too early" and reject the whole game. He says the cynic's belief is self-fulfilling.
- Most effort around wealth goes into siphoning and defending it. He notes there are six times as many parasite species as standalone ones. Societies with too many people slicing the pie rather than baking it collapse.
- He argues crony outcomes such as bank bailouts are government intervention, not free-market capitalism. Capitalism is the minimum set of rules that channels energy into creating property instead of stealing it, and its basis is respect for private property.
- He says this is the greatest period for wealth creation in history, with more knowledge, capital and leverage than ever. Someone moderately intelligent, hardworking and flexible can do very well. Luck exists, but "life is long. People are very consistent. Compounding does work."
- The payoff comes on a 10-to-30-year timescale, "not two years." He says "there's no get-rich quick schemes. That's just someone selling you something."
- On Taleb's skin in the game: if you take a risk, you bear it. Good risk-takers survive and spread the benefits, and bad ones are weeded out through lost capital, lives or reputations. He says the most ethical thing you can do is be an entrepreneur who bears risk.
- He agrees with Buffett and Munger's unease about investment banks going public. The partnership structure made partners bear the risk, while a corporate liability shield lets risk be pushed onto society.
- He sees size as the biggest impediment to progress. Groups seek consensus, not truth, and "don't admit mistakes." The best conditions are small teams, small companies and city-states competing non-violently, each bearing its own results. He cites US federalism and market competition as the model, and says the system breaks with monopolies, captured regulators and central control.
- On alignment: incentive alignment, such as giving someone equity, is real. Other forms of alignment among strangers boil down to coercion, so he calls AI alignment "a joke."

chunks.heading: Good products are hard to vary, and technology has winner-take-all dynamics
chunks.text:
- Applying Deutsch's "hard to vary" test to products: a good product's parts interlock so that you can't change or remove one without breaking it, like a puzzle piece that could only have fit one way.
- His examples are the iPhone's form factor, largely unchanged since its 2007 launch, and the laptop. Cars converge on one shape because of wind-tunnel testing.
- Simple means elegant, not simplistic: remove what's unnecessary. He quotes Saint-Exupéry on the airplane wing, perfect when there's "nothing left to take away."
- Emergence comes from constraints, not freedom. Locking parts together creates a new capability, as with a company or a contract.
- His rule on variants: "if you're selling multiple versions of your product, you better have a really good reason for that."
- Technology is "the automation of knowledge." You figure something out, automate it, scale it and distribute it. The embedded knowledge is persistent because it rests on a good explanation. Once battery knowledge existed, electric cars became close to inevitable.
- Good products have surprising reach. The iPhone's creators didn't plan it for oil companies. Blackberry/enterprise went the same way: Steve Ballmer-era skepticism said enterprise wouldn't tolerate a phone without a keyboard. But employees brought iPhones from home and "the IT guys got outvoted."
- All technology has deeply winner-take-all network effects and scale economies. The best product amortizes development over the largest user base. Even Amazon was not expected to have a network effect.
- Internet markets end up with one huge winner plus a long tail of small players, and they "destroy the mediocre middle." The middle relied on geography or regulation.
- Money can't buy a better phone or, in his view, a better car than the Tesla Model Y (as of 2025). Expensive cars are "just weirder," and trying to buy status is the worst way to signal it.

chunks.heading: Judgment, taste and learning from the specific to the general
chunks.text:
- He favors learning from the specific to the general, citing Seneca. Do things in reality, test them, then generalize. This tells you when a maxim applies and when it doesn't. Academia does the reverse, producing what Taleb calls an "intellectual yet idiot": overeducated and underpracticed.
- "If you want to be a philosopher king, first be a king." Elon's principle of speed came from doing, with concrete implementations like engineers setting their own requirements and unblocking everything.
- His reading habits changed. He used to read hundreds or thousands of books and now thinks most of that was worthless. He reads deliberately and in small amounts, to spark thinking. He rereads *Skin in the Game* because it generalizes things he's noticed, such as the minority rule. He doesn't use Taleb's antifragility because he finds few real applications.
- Judgment is the key skill in an age of infinite leverage. His example: two Apple CEO candidates, one right 80% of the time and one 85%. You'd pay the second billions more per year because he steers a multi-trillion-dollar ship.
- Judgment comes from experience plus honest reflection. Eventually it becomes so good it can't be articulated, and that is taste: "it doesn't feel right to me." Examples are Rick Rubin, Steve Jobs, and AI researchers deciding which experiments to run.
- On the "10,000 hours" idea, he says it is really about iterations, not repetitions. You do something, honestly reflect on the outcome, change something, and try again. Do that enough and your judgment develops.
- His investing is now "almost entirely" taste. He passes when he doesn't want to take a walk with the founder, isn't curious about the category, or doesn't want to be associated with how the money is made. He wants to work with people who are capable, low-ego and intelligent.
- His line on diligence: what you do and who you do it with matter more than how hard you work, but you still have to work as hard as you can.
- Deep problems take intense focus and time. He describes 24-to-36-hour compiler-writing sessions in college, and breakthroughs that come an hour after he's ready to hang up with his co-founder. His technique is to load a problem into the subconscious so insight arrives later. He quotes John Cleese: "let your mind rest against the problem in a friendly, persistent way."
- He says that if work feels forced, you lose to someone for whom it's fun.

chunks.heading: AI, leverage and entrepreneurs
chunks.text:
- AI is "the ultimate leverage information retrieval tool," not a source of judgment. It gives the conventional correct answer for solved problems and is good "when wrong answers are okay."
- Because everyone gets the same AI answer, there's no edge in it. The edge comes from early adoption and from using it on bleeding-edge problems.
- His quip: "It's not that AI is going to replace software engineers, [it's that] AI is going to let software engineers replace everybody else." He says people claiming programming is dead are "idiots." As evidence he cites Mark Zuckerberg paying hundred-million-dollar packages to individual machine learning engineers.
- Structured thinking still matters. Jobs's team built the iPhone because they understood what was possible across materials, manufacturing, supply chains, costing, batteries and bandwidth. Even with AI doing the vibe coding, building something new requires understanding the abstraction the AI is hiding, where it errs and how the pieces fit.
- AI handles what's been done before, and "you can't get paid in any meaningful way for things that have already been done before."
- Good entrepreneurs hate doing the same thing day after day. He calls that "a failure of automation and a failure of imagination." No entrepreneur is replaced by AI; they may be replaced by another entrepreneur who uses it better.
- He hopes for 7 billion companies, one per person, as tools make entrepreneurship broadly accessible.

chunks.heading: Building the new company and funding
chunks.text:
- His new company is called Impossible Inc. (impossiblecomputer.com), still in stealth. He says it is probably the hardest thing he's tried. Four technical experts he spoke to each called it impossible, "for four completely different reasons."
- It is funded with his own money, burning "a million and a half dollars a month." He says that cost is a motivator: "a big carrot and a big stick."
- He has never learned faster, because he's motivated by a concrete build. His tactics: pull up the papers, interrogate ChatGPT (o3 Pro) and Gemini 2.5 Pro, and run whiteboard sessions with his co-founder, asking the "idiot" questions.
- He describes the co-founder as brilliant, low-ego and hardworking ("if he's awake, he's working").
- Early recruiting lessons from his experience:
  - Don't recruit high-ego people even if they're good.
  - Don't oversell, because it comes unstuck later.
  - Hire more technical builders early and fewer marketers, since otherwise you create too many requirements too early.
- On funding, he argues the biggest companies were mostly self-financed or broke out early. Apple, Tesla and SpaceX were self-financed. Google, Microsoft and Amazon took small checks after reaching escape velocity, and Facebook got profitable quickly. Round after round of venture capital rarely builds iconic companies. He calls this a heresy.
- On Elon's story (which he says may be apocryphal): after PayPal he put roughly $100M into SpaceX, $80M into Tesla and $20M into SolarCity. He cites Fred Smith of FedEx and Steve Jobs funding Pixar and NeXT as similar cases. His takeaway is "you have to have the courage of your convictions when nobody else does" and cross the gap from zero to one.
- Naval says he is in "endgame content" mode: with little to lose, he can play without fear. He thinks Jobs and Elon built from inspiration, not fear.
- He criticizes VCs who call themselves "the team behind the team." In his view the founder takes the risk and built the company.

chunks.heading: Pursuing outcomes indirectly and choosing what to want
chunks.text:
- He says the elusive goals are elusive because they are best pursued indirectly:
  - Wealth: someone who is really into the work outcompetes someone who isn't. Purely selfish industries such as porn, gambling and crypto casinos don't attract the best teams.
  - Happiness: direct pursuit of pleasure leads to addiction and dopamine burnout.
  - Status: it is a hidden hierarchy, and claiming it lowers it. Trying to tear others down is covert status-seeking.
  - Love: giving love is what you want, not needing to receive it.
- He applies Deutsch's "fun criterion": if you're not having fun, don't do it. He doesn't follow it all the way, for example with teaching children math.
- Explore, then invest. Explore widely to find the fit, because there's near-infinite optionality. But "all the benefits in life come from compound interest," so once you've found the fit you must invest in a job, place, people, business and health. People often under-explore on jobs (three weeks looking, five years in the role).
- His test of intelligence: "the only true test of intelligence is if you get what you want out of life." It has two parts: choosing what to want, and getting it.
- Choose inspiration over envy. He draws on Elon and Peter Thiel without swapping lives with anyone.
- Virtues are long-term selfishness. His line is "the modern devil is cheap dopamine." He recommends starting charity locally: help people near you, because "your family is broken, but you're going to fix the world."
- A mission larger than yourself pulls people together as a Schelling point, as with SpaceX's Mars goal, but only "on your own terms." He later says the tweet to follow is "live for something larger than yourself, but only on your own terms."
- His summary routine tweet: "Fast, lift, sprint, stretch, and meditate. Build, sell, write, create, invest, and own. Productize yourself. Build or buy equity in a business. Read, reflect, love, seek truth, and ignore society. Make these habits. Say no to everything else. Avoid debt, jail, addiction, disgrace, shortcuts, and media." The sign-off is "Relax. Victory is assured."
- His view on the ordering of wealth, health and happiness: pursue wealth when young (teens learn and do, 20s work hard, 30s harvest), then protect health and work on happiness. In importance the order reverses. He says an amazing life is 70 to 80% in each category rather than 150 in one and zero in another.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Naval says his real expertise is taking a specific technology business apart and predicting what will work, not abstract wealth advice. He explains power-law outcomes, common founder mistakes, and why understanding, judgment and taste matter more than memorization in the age of AI.

chunks.heading: Naval's specific knowledge is analyzing technology businesses
chunks.text:
- Naval says his specific knowledge is not happiness or philosophy. It is taking a technology business "apart at the seams" and predicting in advance what is likely to work and what is not.
- He says business is "very, very contextual". You have to look at the particular business, understand what is being done, why and how, then tear it apart and reassemble it properly.
- He admits he will be wrong most of the time ("Clubhouse notwithstanding"). It is like playing the lottery, except you know one or two of the ticket numbers in advance.
- He says this is why talking about wealth in the abstract is hard. Abstract advice has to be right in every context, so it shrinks to timeless statements. Specific advice, applied to a real business and a real entrepreneur, is where the real knowledge is.
- He admits "How to Get Rich" is a deliberately clickbait title. The thread was short and crafted, and left "10,000 things" on the cutting room floor.

chunks.heading: Power law outcomes: you only need to be right a few times
chunks.text:
- Naval says you operate in a "highly leveraged intellectual domain", so outcomes are nonlinear.
- In any power law distribution, number one returns more than two through n put together. Number two returns more than three through n put together.
- His example is Peter Thiel. He started PayPal but made his big money on Facebook, which was the big winner.
- Implication: you only have to be right a few times, or even once, to get the big score.

chunks.heading: Red flags Naval looks for when taking a startup apart
chunks.text:
When he has a specific entrepreneur and business in front of him, he checks for these:

- **Wrong reasons:** "You're doing A so you can get to B. Just go to B."
- **Money vs. love of the product:** if the founder is in it for money, the person who builds it because they love the product will beat them.
- **Wrong investors:** raising money from people who are in it for the wrong reasons.
- **Wrong co-founder:** a co-founder who is not in it for the right reasons, or the wrong kind of co-founder.
- **Structure mistakes:** a wrong vesting schedule.
- **Wrong place:** starting the business in the wrong location.
- **Wrong angle:** approaching the problem from this angle instead of that one.
- He grants he will be wrong sometimes too, but says he has seen a lot of data and has his theories.

chunks.heading: Understanding, judgment and taste beat memorization
chunks.text:
- Naval's heuristic: "If you have to memorize something, it's because you don't understand it. And if you understand something, you don't have to memorize it."
- Real understanding lets you re-derive what you need from first principles. Each piece of knowledge works like a Lego block that locks into a steel frame.
- Memorization is worth less every day. ChatGPT has memorized the internet, and you will not beat it, a library or any 10 books at memorization.
- What matters now is understanding, judgment and taste.
- Those come from having real problems, solving them, and finding the commonalities across them.
- This is why he prefers podcasts to tweets. Deep understanding lets you talk about a topic for hours. Aphorisms are now copied by thousands of people and by ChatGPT.
- He does not want abstract talk. He wants to work through an actual business with an actual problem and solve it.

chunks.heading: Mastery in any field leads to philosophy
chunks.text:
- Naval defines philosophy as finding the hidden generalizable truths among specific experiences, then using them as heuristics for future ones.
- Any subject pursued deeply enough ends in philosophy, and mastery of anything makes you a philosopher. You find unity in anything if you go deep enough.
- This is why timeless advice keeps looking like cliché. It is cliché "for reasons".
- Philosophy can still progress. Scientific advances changed outlooks, such as a geocentric universe vs. a vast one, or gods vs. computable laws of physics.
- Moral philosophy has also advanced. He cites the near-universal abandonment of slavery.

chunks.heading: Answer questions at the level at which they are asked
chunks.text:
- Naval says many philosophical paradoxes come from switching scale. This idea draws on David Deutsch and his friend James Pierce.
- **Meaning:** asked by Chris, here and now, there is meaning. Answered from the universe's view over infinite time (heat death), there is none. Do not ask as a human and answer as God.
- **Free will:** asked by an individual, yes. Your mind-body system cannot predict what you will do next, and everyone treats each other as having free will. From the block-universe view of particle collisions, no.
- His rule: "Answer at the level at which it was asked." Many paradoxes dissolve when you do.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Naval says he now sees himself as a builder, choosing hard hardware problems over easy market bets. He argues AI incumbents are incentivized to pull up the ladder, that open models are the answer to centralization, and that network effects make naive free-trade logic fail. He frames jobs as opportunities and wealth as capital plus knowledge.

chunks.heading: From investor to hardware builder: Naval's career and what Air Chat taught him
chunks.text:
- Naval now calls himself a builder of things. He treats investing as a side hobby and says "every so-called career is an evolution" toward whatever interests you most.
- His path: Venture Hacks, then AngelList, with early investments including Twitter, Uber and Notion. He says he is not especially proud of being an investor.
- He built Air Chat, an audio-first, Twitter-like social product with AI transcription and translation. It never took off, and because it was a social product it needed to catch on to work.
- He is still proud of the product and the team. The team was paid, and the investors he brought in got their money back.
- Lesson he took: he enjoys designing every pixel of a product and getting it to market. His next company is harder, combining hardware and software.
- He now wants to take more technical risk than market risk. Elon Musk is his inspiration for building hard, useful things. He cites Peter Thiel's idea that the future has to be built.
- He is cautious about the new product. He says it is "really hard" and he is not sure he can pull it off.
- He says the new company depends on AI, and so did Air Chat. Without AI transcription and translation, Air Chat could not have existed.
- AngelList is also adopting AI heavily.

chunks.heading: Why Naval started tweeting, and what made his writing spread
chunks.text:
- The AngelList idea of matching investors to startups did not work as a business. It had started as an email list that was popular early and then stalled.
- The SEC then sent a letter saying he was acting as an unlicensed dealer. He says he earned no money from it and treated it as a public service.
- He went to Washington and got the law changed. He says this paved the way for ICOs, incubators and demo days.
- The period was highly stressful, and he began tweeting the realizations he was having under that pressure.
- His recurring themes were science (he is an amateur physics fan), philosophy and making money. His Twitter bio joke was "truth, love and money".
- Why it resonated: everyone thinks about everything, not just their narrow lane. People deal with their relationships, with the universe and what is true, and with the practical business of earning a living.
- Before this, people expected someone in his position to talk only about money and stay in his lane.
- Many of his best pieces were notes to self, reminders such as "don't forget this".
- The "How to Get Rich" thread was one of his earliest and is still among Twitter's most viral threads.
- He prefers timeless topics and philosophy. He compares it to "compound interest in ideas". He avoids news when he can.

chunks.heading: Naval's view on AI policy and the Vance speech
chunks.text:
- He found Vance's speech humble, optimistic and forward-looking. He thinks America should win and should not regulate AI.
- The speech marked a break because earlier events were framed around AI safety: Bletchley Park, the EU regulations and Biden's executive order. It put opportunity first.
- Naval does not believe AI will destroy the world. He compares the doom narrative to a religious belief in the same family as climate, asteroid and Covid doom. He says that kind of fear captures everyone's attention.
- The incentive problem: companies that are ahead want to pull the ladder up behind them. He thinks they probably believe in the safety risks, but they are also motivated to believe them and spread the message.
- He points to a contradiction in their position: it is too dangerous for open source, yet not too dangerous for one private company to own it. If AI were really a Manhattan Project making nuclear weapons, you would not want a single company owning it.
- He cites Sam Altman's remark that AI would capture the "light cone" of all future value. If that is true, open-source and small-tech AI matter a great deal.
- The hard part is that training is naturally centralized because it needs supercomputer clusters. It is unclear how a decentralized model competes.
- His framing of the real problem: how to advance AI without handing control to a few people.
- His biggest fear is not AI itself. It is what a handful of people controlling AI would do to everyone "for our own good", since that is what always happens.
- On OpenAI's structure, he says the company needs to raise money and incentivize staff. But he does not see why it has to buy out the nonprofit entirely.
- His alternative: keep the nonprofit with a truly independent board, and add an incentive package for staff and investors plus a fundraising plan.
- If you want to capture the value of superintelligence, you know it is worth far more than the number being offered.

chunks.heading: AI, jobs and opportunity
chunks.text:
- He agrees with Sacks that there is no evidence yet of mass job destruction from AI. He expects it to create jobs and opportunity at least as fast as it destroys them.
- He objects to the word "jobs". A job means someone else hands you work, which frames it as a zero-sum game. He prefers to talk about opportunities.
- Examples he gives: YouTube streamers and influencers, which were not professions before. Since Covid, many people earn money from home online in ways that are hard to categorize.
- Forecasting trap: he says the European approach wrongly assumes you can predict the future precisely enough to regulate against its risks today. "We don't know enough yet."
- He describes current AI as natural-language computers. People who feared computers no longer need to program in arcane languages or learn obscure math, because they can simply talk to the machine. "The new programming language is English."
- He says many of the jobs at risk are paperwork jobs, often make-work that just shuffles paper. He uses the federal government as his example, joking that a third of it digs holes with spoons and another third fills them in.
- Startups: he notes that new companies are possible that could not have existed without AI. He dismisses Twitter claims like "AGI is here, I fired my mid-level engineers, I stopped hiring" as foolishness.
- The two real stories he sees are entrepreneurs scaling wildly with AI, and employers who want to hire people who are fluent in AI.
- On AGI: he does not think anyone knows how to build it yet, and he sees what exists today as language models used mainly for search and homework.

chunks.heading: Open vs closed AI, DeepSeek, and who wins
chunks.text:
- DeepSeek shows the stakes. You cannot stop the flow of chips and talent, because constrained competitors simply become more efficient.
- He notes China sent America's best open-source model back to it while US labs were going closed source "for safety".
- He agrees America should win, but says the best way to win is to be as open, broad and innovative as possible. One company controlling everything will innovate more slowly than a dynamic, open ecosystem.
- Network effects mean being open still lets the leader win. His example is the internet: it is an open technology, yet the dominant companies are almost all American because the US led.
- He applies the same logic to AI. Open models will spread to China and India, but the leader still benefits.

chunks.heading: Tariffs, network effects and strategic industries
chunks.text:
- Naval's argument is that the textbook Ricardian view (produce what you are best at, trade, and keep tariffs low even if others tax you) ignores that most modern businesses have network effects or economies of scale.
- His thought experiment, with himself as China and the other side as the US:
  - Subsidize the industries that have network effects or winner-take-all dynamics: TikTok, semiconductors, drones, BYD and autos.
  - Ban the other country's social media while spreading yours.
  - Once you win, you own the market and can raise prices. A latecomer cannot start a competitor.
  - Or, with economies of scale, cut prices to zero to drive rivals out, so nobody sane invests, then raise them again.
- His conclusion: these industries are high-margin and sticky. If someone subsidizes them or raises tariffs against you to build them, you have to respond. "You can't just stand back completely."
- Beyond money, he argues tariffs protect a functioning middle class with good jobs. In a world without tariffs the gains might flow only to the upper and lower classes.
- Strategic example: DJI is arguably the world's biggest defense contractor. Both sides in Ukraine source drone parts that trace back to it, and the US lacks that industry.
- He says drones are autonomous bullets and the future of warfare. A drone supply chain means motors, semiconductors, optics and lasers, so there is a strong case to bring at least parts of these industries home.
- He thinks the US is lucky to be nearly self-sufficient, with oil, gas, fracking and nuclear fission, and should be energy self-sufficient with a large surplus.
- He argues that building hard things at scale for national security and innovation is better work than writing essays or doing paperwork, and even better than driving.

chunks.heading: Immigration, knowledge and copyright
chunks.text:
- Naval is a first-generation immigrant who came at 9. He supports skilled, legal immigration where people assimilate, and he distinguishes it sharply from open borders.
- His reasoning: technology drives economic power, military power and even culture. Wealth is capital combined with knowledge, and knowledge is the biggest component. Bringing in the best and brightest made the US the center of knowledge creation.
- He says part of the DeepSeek outcome comes from the US educating talented people and then sending them home.
- On AI copyright, he takes a "riskier" position and largely agrees that scraping the open web to build direct substitutes goes too far. Users now start and end everything inside the model.
- His rule: if you train on the open web, your model should be open source.
- He sees only two stable outcomes:
  - Pay copyright owners. He thinks this won't work on its own, because someone in China will crawl and release weights, which are compressed data.
  - If you crawl, keep the result open and contribute to open source, and let those who don't want to be crawled protect their data.
- He notes that the lossy-compression view of LLMs, attributed to Ilya Sutskever, is central to the fair-use question of whether a model learns or just regurgitates.

chunks.heading: Personal operating habits Naval mentions
chunks.text:
- Parenting: he follows David Deutsch's idea of taking children seriously and giving them the same freedom as an adult. He credits Aaron Stupple as an explainer of the approach but says Aaron's near-total version is not his own position.
- His own rules: each child does 1 hour of math or programming and 2 hours of reading a day, and after that they are free. Everything else is persuasion, not control.
- He homeschools his children, and says that to raise capable adults you want them to make their own decisions.
- Sleep: he sits in bed and meditates. His reasoning is that the mind dislikes meditation so much that, forced to choose between meditating and sleeping, it falls asleep.
- Naval avoids mentally heavy or existential conversations before bed.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Naval explains how coding agents like Claude Code and Codex hit an inflection point in late 2025, letting a non-coder one-shot custom apps and build a personal app store. He argues pure software is no longer venture investable, that human operators must still guide agents, and that tiny teams can now scale to huge outcomes.

chunks.heading: Vibe coding as a new way to build software (Dec 2025 inflection)
chunks.text:
- Naval says coding agents hit an inflection point around December 2025 with the release of Claude Opus 4.5. He describes it as "a junior programmer at your disposal who's fast, essentially free, and ready to please."
- He hadn't seriously coded in decades, despite a computer science degree. The activation energy was high: you had to connect GitHub, a backend (Vercel, Firebase, Railway) and many other tools, and know the jargon.
- Agents remove that barrier. They run in a text-based command line (CLI) on top of Unix, which is the bulk of what they were trained on. They can run shell commands, use the file system, call grep, awk and sed, run cron jobs so they live long, and spawn more tasks.
- They work as translators from English to Python, C, Rust and other languages. They tolerate misspellings and loose wording.
- A high-level grasp of computer architecture, networking and programming is enough to go "very, very far."
- He started with Claude Code and uses Codex for thornier bugs and deep problems.
- He found it addictive, and compares it to a video game. A game is bounded, with fake rewards, and gets boring once you learn its rules. Vibe coding is unbounded because "you've got a Turing machine running underneath." You set the objective, and the results matter in the real world.
- He now spends a couple of hours most nights on it. That time used to go to reading, doom scrolling or games. It is also why he has been absent from X.

chunks.heading: Building exactly what you want without team compromise
chunks.text:
- You need a clear direction. "You have to know what you want. That's actually the hardest thing."
- Naval got his clarity from Airchat, a voice and video social messenger he built for about a year. It didn't work, so the company was sold, investors got their money back and the team got "nice packages."
- He had 8 or 9 engineers and 9 to 12 months, and shipped a couple of variations.
- He is now rebuilding that app from scratch with no compromises. With a team you always accommodate people, even as the "dictator." You can't tell an engineer "Move this icon left. Now move it right. Now move it back" on gut feel alone.
- An AI agent is like a self-driving car with no driver, so you don't feel self-conscious about your idiosyncrasies.
- Expected result: fast prototypes that are true to one creator's vision, with possibly weak code quality, architecture, security and scaling. He compares it to Notch coding Minecraft alone. Its blocky graphics looked like a step backwards, but he never had to explain them to anyone.
- He thinks it expands discovery. The share of people who might build apps goes from about 0.1% to 1-3% of the population. Most people will still see computers as a black box.
- It suits people who are creative, self-motivated and articulate, with a good vision.
- To scale a high-functioning app to many users, he says to recruit a great team and real engineers, and "you're probably going to have to rewrite the whole thing." For experimenting and prototyping, he says there is nothing better.
- He says it has "never been a better time to be alive as a creator of software."

chunks.heading: Personal app store and custom apps
chunks.text:
- Naval built an app store just for himself. It is a web page, later an app on his iPhone. He asks Claude for an app, it ships to the store, and he installs it with one click and gets upgrades.
- Workflow: open Claude on the phone, either a remote terminal on his desktop or Claude in the cloud. Claude connects to Xcode. He gives a two-line description and about 30 seconds after the install he has a working app.
- Example: a custom workout tracker. He told it to:
  - Use the functionality of Tonal and Ladder.
  - Follow Apple's human interface guidelines.
  - Import a text log of his recent workouts.
  - Make re-entry and adjustment easy.
  - Build charts and strength scores by body part, based on scientific papers.
  - Show a human body diagram.
  - Connect to Apple Health for heart rate.
- He says a lot of that went into one prompt, and a working app arrived immediately.
- Limits: Apple gates distribution. Apps must be keyed to specific devices, so he can share with friends and family but not everyone.
- Broad-use-case apps still win where hand-tuned products cover your need. Custom apps are best for niche, private or highly personal needs.
- Use case: at dinner, someone describes an app they want, and 5 minutes later you can show it on your phone.

chunks.heading: Pure software is uninvestable; where value moves
chunks.text:
- Naval's stronger version of his tweet is "pure software is uninvestable." Full stop.
- Reason 1: people can hack the software together today.
- Reason 2: coding agents improve so fast that within a year or less they will probably build scalable software with good architecture.
- If your advantage is "I'm building cool software other people don't know how to build," he calls that uninvestable.
- Venture investors should now look for hardware, network effects and AI models. He argues training AI models is "the new building software," for as long as that lasts before auto research and auto training work.
- He is unsure whether market opportunities favor incumbents (distribution plus the ability to fill every gap) or are open to newcomers. He leans toward a renaissance for individual software creators.
- One- and two-person software companies can scale to millions of users and billions of dollars. Precedents: Notch, Satoshi Nakamoto, the original Instagram and WhatsApp teams. He expects more of them.
- He says "careers are kind of dead," but that you can create interesting opportunities by building and learning at the frontier.

chunks.heading: Why agents will displace the app-and-phone model (Apple thesis)
chunks.text:
- His March 23 tweet: AI coding agents can deliver one-shot custom apps to your phone, "the beginning of the end for the iPhone's dominance."
- Apple's margins depend on its OS and apps being better than everyone else's. The hardware is better but doesn't support those margins.
- As people talk to agents ("call me an Uber," "track my workout") instead of tapping through apps, the phone matters less. Agents can build their own APIs on the fly, so they don't need app APIs.
- A phone then needs only a screen, battery and connectivity, so Android is as good as an iPhone. Apple now uses Google's Gemini.
- Interfaces get generated on the fly. Tapping through menus and hunting for buttons should become conversational and agentic.
- Apple would compete on chips and integrated hardware, at margins closer to Samsung or Lenovo. He expects its market cap to compress.
- He thinks Apple giving up on AI "will go down as the biggest strategic mistake in the tech industry of this decade."
- Analogy: Microsoft is worth more than ever but lost the Windows battle by missing mobile and focusing on enterprise. Apple can stay valuable but be "a lot less valuable than it could have been."

chunks.heading: Operating coding agents: oversight, limits and multi-model use
chunks.text:
- Agents still need a human operator. Naval says to guide architecture, debugging and features, and watch closely.
- Context limits: state of the art is about a million tokens. As a codebase outgrows the context window, models guess, compact, lose the plot, fix the wrong thing, fix the same bug five times and patch instead of fixing the architecture.
- Boneheaded behavior: they may fix a bug by deleting the feature or write a hack. He often stops the model and says "that's a hack... Go fix it at an architectural level." The model always answers "You're right," even when it wasn't a hack.
- He compares the model to a dog. It is better than you at catching the duck, but "it's still a dog" and may take down the wrong bird.
- They are sycophantic. If you lean toward an answer, they find it, and you would have to be "pretty wrong" for them to contradict you.
- Multi-agent councils help less than expected. Instances of one model share the same data and "brain," so ten talking to each other just adds ten times the tokens. He wires GitHub so Codex and Gemini automatically review pull requests that Claude writes, but finds "a lot of groupthink."
- His view of the models' strengths:
  - Claude: artifacts and visual presentation, and it meets you at your level.
  - ChatGPT: "the OG," good all around.
  - Gemini: search (Google index) and YouTube data. He calls the product frustrating, with timeouts and lost context.
  - Grok: least nerfed, tells the truth, X access for news, strong on deep scientific and math problems.
- Today you can one-shot simple apps such as a task list or a video game clone. He expects complex apps to follow as data grows.

chunks.heading: Why AI is good at coding, and self-fixing app workflows
chunks.text:
- Models excel where there is a lot of data and outputs are easy to verify. Code has to compile, execute and pass pre-written tests. Math and self-driving are similar.
- They do worse in brand-new fields with little data, which leaves room for human creativity. They also do worse where quality is hard to verify, such as creative writing, since graders are only as good as their taste.
- He thinks coding models improved recently partly because top software engineers started using them and fed their taste back in. "You need high taste feedback loops to improve these models."
- Automated bug loop in his own app:
  - A user taps a button on a bug and logs are sent to a server.
  - Every 24 hours Claude goes through all reports and fixes them on side branches.
  - Naval reviews each fix and decides "ship it" or "don't ship that." He acts as the final gate.
- He expects this to extend to features: users request and vote, and a tastemaker or maintainer in the cloud filters them. He sees agents as "perfect customer service" that are also coders, available 24/7 and with no ego about discarding code.
- Kids learn well from vibe coding because of instant feedback and rewards. They are forced to pick up the command line, architecture, caching, backing off, streams, disk writes and latency versus bandwidth.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: In the first half of this Tim Ferriss combo episode, Naval explains why honesty and presence are core values, what he screens for in founders (intelligence, energy, integrity), and how he builds skills and habits instead of chasing epiphanies. He also covers reading old source books, choiceless-awareness meditation, and desire as a contract for unhappiness. The second half is Nick Kokonas and is excluded.

chunks.heading: What Naval looks for in founders: intelligence, energy, integrity
chunks.text:
Naval screens founders on three traits, plus one personal test.

- **Intelligence.** Founders must know what they are doing. This is a fuzzy judgment, formed from conversation. He asks whether they have insight and specific knowledge, and whether they have thought about the problem deeply. It is not about age or years of experience, only the depth of their understanding of what they are about to do.
- **Energy.** Being a founder is "brutally difficult" and takes a long time, and in the long run the people who succeed are the ones who persevere. Red flags are founders who run out of energy, who work in a hesitant, preliminary way, who constantly seek positive feedback, or who are easily thrown off course.
- **Integrity.** Intelligence and energy without integrity gives you "a hardworking smart crook". Startups are fast-moving and people are independent, so anyone who wants to screw you over will find a way. His definition: "ethics and integrity are what you do despite the money. If being ethical was profitable everybody would do it."
- **Integrity red flag.** A founder who offers to do something slightly unfair to another shareholder, employee or founder in order to please Naval. If they will do it to them, they will do it to him. Integrity is the hardest trait to judge because it takes longitudinal, long-term relationships.
- **Personal test.** Investing in or founding with someone means having them in your life for about a decade. Naval only works with people he genuinely likes. If a call or meeting with them is exhausting, or they are negative or difficult, "no amount of money is worth it". He and Tim "will both die with money in the bank", so the question is whether he wants to spend scarce time and mental energy on these people.
- **Favorite founders.** The ones he learns from. When they call for help he jumps on it, because an hour walking around the block with them leaves him smarter.

chunks.heading: Honesty as a core operating value
chunks.text:
Naval treats honesty as a foundational value, for three reasons.

- **Physics.** Feynman said "you must never ever fool yourself, and you are the easiest person to fool". In physics you don't negotiate or soften things to make people feel better, because a wrong equation simply won't work.
- **Street honesty.** Growing up in New York, he saw members of the Russian mob take each other's word even while ready to kill each other. That showed him how much relationships depend on honesty.
- **Presence.** Withholding or lying, even a white lie, creates "a second thread" in your head that must keep tracking what you said versus what you think. That pulls you out of the present moment and creates stress and distraction over time.
- **Recommended book.** *Lying* by Sam Harris, on deceit in general, including white lies meant to protect people.

chunks.heading: Investing is an emotional skill built through internal work
chunks.text:
- Naval says the way to improve at investing is to work on your internal state until you are free of as many biases and conditioned responses as you can be.
- Investors only pretend to be rational. They decide whether they want to invest in the first five minutes of a meeting. If a company doesn't take their money in the first round, they get annoyed, and they have to undo that emotional state so they can still be a positive force when the second round comes.
- He rejects "the Epiphany theory of self-development". Reading one book or phrase and pinning it to your screen doesn't change you. Happiness, nutrition, diet, investing and self-awareness are all skills, built over decades through feedback loops.
- Books that shaped him: Seneca and Marcus Aurelius' *Meditations* (an emperor's private diary showing that power and success don't fix your internal state), Sam Harris, Jiddu Krishnamurti's *The Book of Life*, and Bruce Lee's writings. He pays attention to "rational Buddhists" and ignores the mysticism and guru worship.

chunks.heading: How Naval reads: treat books like disposable blog posts
chunks.text:
- **The problem.** Twitter and Facebook gave him "little dopamine snacks" without real learning. Books felt sacred and had to be finished, so people got stuck on them and stopped reading.
- **Old problems.** For old problems, such as health, calm, values and raising a family, older sources are more reliable, because a book that survived 2,000 years has been filtered by many people. For new problems, such as driving a car or flying a plane, read modern sources.
- **Go to the source.** For example, *Origin of Species* is cheap on Kindle and an easy read, and almost nothing in it is incorrect.
- **The hack.** Treat books as throwaway blog posts or tweets and feel no obligation to finish any of them.
  - He buys any book that someone mentions.
  - He reads 10 to 20 books at a time and flips through them.
  - He skips ahead, starts in the middle where a paragraph catches his eye, and deletes books that bore him or contain errors.
- **Result.** Books are back in his reading library, and with them a lot of ancient wisdom.

chunks.heading: Habits, skills and building a sustainable life
chunks.text:
- Naval says we are "a collection of thousands, maybe tens of thousands of habits" running subconsciously, leaving a little extra neocortex for new problems. "You become your habits."
- A light daily workout from his trainer showed him how much habits change you physically and mentally. His view is that "to have peace of mind you have to have peace of body first".
- **Operating rule.** In any six-month window he is either picking up a good habit or dropping a bad one. Real change such as getting fit is a 10-year journey, not a three-month fix.
- **Sustainability.** He wants everything and doesn't want to suffer through deprivation. For diet, he changes his taste buds to like healthier foods and substitutes tasty healthy foods for unhealthy ones. He wants a life that is effortless, so a habit must be sustainable with no effort.

chunks.heading: Success, desire and the three options
chunks.text:
- **Success.** Naval admires creators and commercializers (Steve Jobs, Marc Andreessen for Netscape, Satoshi Nakamoto, Elon Musk). But he thinks the real winners are the ones who step out of the game entirely and need nothing from anyone. A test he cites: if you can sit quietly in a room for 30 minutes and be happy, you are successful.
- **Desire.** "Desire is a contract you make with yourself to be unhappy until you get what you want." He chooses desires carefully and tries to hold no more than one big desire at a time. He sees desire as the axis of his suffering.
- **Three options in any situation.** You can change it, accept it, or leave it. Wishing you could change it or leave it, without doing either and without accepting it, causes most misery. The word he tells himself most often is "accept".
- **Advice to his younger self.** Chill out, don't stress so much, and be more yourself. Don't live up to other people's expectations. Say no to more things and protect your time, because the marginal value of an extra day rises as you age.
- **Love.** Love can't be bought, but it is free to give. Quoting Charlie Munger's "be worthy of a mate", he says to work on yourself until you no longer need things, and then they appear.

chunks.heading: Choiceless awareness: his meditation method
chunks.text:
- Naval says most people claim to meditate but few actually do. The form that works for him is "choiceless awareness" (non-judgmental awareness), which he pieced together from Krishnamurti.
- You walk around your day, ideally near nature and not in conversation, and accept the moment without judging anything or anyone. He runs his brain "in debugger mode" and watches his thoughts.
- Enlightenment is "a space between your thoughts", which you can achieve moment to moment.
- When he traces his thoughts, about 90% turn out to be fear-based and the other 10% desire-based. Desire is fear by another name. Once a thought is recognized as fear it fades, the mind quiets, and he stops taking his life for granted.
- Ten to fifteen minutes of this leaves him peaceful and grateful.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Naval tells interns the biggest compounding decisions are what you work on and who you work with, and that networking should happen through work, not mingling. He describes how he runs his new company: tiny team, high pay, slow hiring, fast firing, no bullets. He also covers leverage, taste as a moat, deep tech, and why feedback from reality beats feedback from graders.

chunks.heading: Choosing where to work: Bay Area, industry, then who you work with
chunks.text:
- Naval says "earn with your mind, not your time" does not mean working less. Hours are capped (168 a week), so the lever is direction. Life compounds, so the big decisions have to be right.
- He treats the Bay Area and tech as "cheat codes". It is the highest concentration of high-IQ, motivated people. He compares it to Athens, Rome, industrial-era Manchester or London, and Paris, where the best people gathered.
- After place and industry, the next decisions are what to work on and who to work with.
  - What to work on: a natural inclination, a deep field, and a secret or specific knowledge (the Peter Thiel sense).
  - Who to work with: the absolute best people.
- He says the biggest early shortcoming is staying limited to whoever happens to be nearby. "Life is a search function", and curating who you work with never stops.
- He dislikes giving advice ("like people telling you their winning lottery ticket numbers"). He does see two consistent themes from successful older people:
  - Who they worked with was the most important factor.
  - They enjoyed the work, because "if you don't enjoy it you're not going to be good".
- These principles are hard in practice because they mean rejecting people and walking away from good situations toward great ones.

chunks.heading: Naval's motivations over time and what actually worked
chunks.text:
- Naval says his bar for who he worked with and whether he enjoyed the work was too low early on.
- His first founder attempts were driven by wanting the "founder" label, not by the company or the people.
- Later he was driven by money and power. He calls these fundamental drivers that nobody wants to admit, and not a great motivation either.
- His best outcomes came from following genuine curiosity. Asking "what's behind this?" repeatedly produced insight, which led to good investments, startups and outcomes.
- Now he doesn't need money or status. He asks:
  - What product does he want to exist?
  - What beautiful thing wouldn't exist without his effort?
  - Which people does he want to spend all day with?
- On meeting material needs: he says that once you don't have to hustle you get bored. Meditating in a corner gets boring, and hedonism is "a death trap". The answer he gives is self-actualization through creating: "it's better to create than to consume".
- He argues that talented, curious, hardworking, high-integrity people he met in his 20s all became successful 20-30 years later, "without exception". He wishes he had invested in or stayed close to every one of them.

chunks.heading: Networking and finding collaborators through work
chunks.text:
- Naval doesn't believe in "empty networking" (mingling, name tags, meeting everyone). Be discriminating and look for earned respect: talent, curiosity, good nature, low ego, high drive and vision.
- Don't hunt for the one future star (the "Dylan Field problem"). That is impossible. Look for like-minded people you learn from, enjoy, and want to stay in touch with.
- He says the best way to match is through work, not talking. Hackathons and small projects are good.
- In any group project, one person usually carries the load. Hopefully that's you. If not, find the person who is number one and make yourself useful to them. "It'll pay off. It just takes a long time."
- His new company, the Impossible Computer Company, was assembled this way.
  - He has worked with one person since they met 20 years ago, and another since his last company about four years ago.
  - His co-founder has strong technical taste. He finds weird, idiosyncratic products, papers or code, understands them deeply, then reaches out. He compliments the creator, offers help, asks good questions, and contributes to the code. Over time this has surrounded him with brilliant, artistic people.
  - The team members see themselves as creators, not as "engineer" or "AI person". They pick up whatever skill is needed, and AI makes that easier. He calls AI an incredible learning engine for autodidacts.

chunks.heading: How Naval runs his company now
chunks.text:
- The team is under 20 people, based in person in SF. A few trusted, long-known people are remote.
- His rule is not to ask anyone to do what he wouldn't do. He wants:
  - The office in a location he likes.
