  - Nice private offices, not cubicles or crammed desks. He calls cramped desks inhuman and says hustle-culture desk grinding is mostly "pretend work".
  - Good pay, lots of stock and high salaries.
  - People always working or thinking about work, the same bar he holds himself to.
- Being older, he says, lets him be more idiosyncratic and do things his way, which he always wanted but lacked the confidence for.
- Unpopular CEO decisions:
  - Fire much faster.
  - Hire much more slowly and resist hiring.
  - "Pay twice as much but expect 10 times the output". He means real output, not hours, because creative domains reward the right decision "infinitely" more.
- On Keith Rabois's barrels versus bullets: barrels decide direction and when to pull the trigger, and bullets get aimed. Big companies split management from execution. Naval says in a small company everyone must be a barrel.
  - They hired a 19-year-old as a full peer: no one tells him what to do, same pay, same output expectation.
  - His co-founder is 23, started working at 15, and has the same stock and authority as Naval.
- On decisions and disputes:
  - No real argument has happened yet, which he admits may be a honeymoon.
  - The person doing the job, especially technical work, usually has the best insight. Disputes get resolved through execution, the way Elon Musk does it ("I'm going to sleep underneath my desk, I'm taking over your job").
  - For fuzzy topics like the product name, he picks the three people with the best taste and has them vote. He warns that too many "marketing droids" make a company go in circles.

chunks.heading: When to quit, and starting deep tech
chunks.text:
- On burnout, Naval rejects the idea that it is temporary and that a two-month break will bring you back better. He says burnout means you no longer enjoy the work and should probably move on.
- He has seen people work around the clock without burning out when they enjoy it and see clear progress in product or deployment. People "burn out" when good people leave and direction is unclear.
- Founders increasingly start deep tech later: Elon (Zip2, X/PayPal, then SpaceX, Tesla, SolarCity), Kyle Vogt (Cruise, then robots), Sam Altman (Loopt, then OpenAI). Naval started in hardware with linear optical amplifiers and is now back in hardware.
- Reasons he gives: software feels saturated and AI makes it easy, SpaceX and OpenAI inspire people, and supply chains make hardware easier than before.
- Upsides of deep tech: a steep learning curve, less competition, and possibly more meaningful work. It also gives a better moat in the age of AI.
- Downsides:
  - It is much harder and the odds of success are lower.
  - Some great-looking products left founders and investors with nothing, because they needed too much money and got wiped out.
  - Products get cloned in China or Korea within a year or two, so there is no way to monetize.
- His advice: go where you are most inspired. If you go deep tech, start early, because failures are more forgivable (he says before about 25), the learning is huge, and you meet hardware contacts for later.

chunks.heading: Taste, strengths and leverage as moats
chunks.text:
- Naval says design is always a moat. Good design needs taste and a good eye.
- AI will fill the world with average, then with extreme, until every permutation exists (he cites Borges's "Library of Babel"). The core task then becomes editing, selection and curation, so develop judgment and taste:
  - Learn what makes things great.
  - Don't dislike something just because someone else made it.
  - Pair taste with hard work to build.
- His own taste came from a youth of reading, including poetry. Twitter's 140 characters forced him to choose words like poetry, and the taste paid off in a way he couldn't have predicted.
- On finding your strength: "I want to work with people better than me" is not enough, because you must bring something unique. Almost everyone is good at an intersection of two or three things (Scott Adams's skill stack).
  - A signal: it feels like play to you, looks like work to others, and impresses them.
  - Don't cover weaknesses. Ally with people strong in them and double down on your strengths.
- On leverage: leverage forms went from labor to capital to media, then code ("permissionless" leverage), and now AI, agents, robots, supply chains and 3D printing.
  - One-person billion-dollar companies already exist: Notch with Minecraft (sold to Microsoft for $2 billion) and Satoshi's Bitcoin.
  - Returns will be non-linear and society isn't built for it. He says it's not the rich getting richer but "the smart and leveraged".
  - Earning power is downstream of knowledge creation and the ability to leverage it.

chunks.heading: Education: what to study and which degrees are worth it
chunks.text:
- Naval says the most useful parts of college were the really hard things, like writing a compiler, which gave him confidence that no computer science problem was beyond him. He wishes he had stuck with physics and math to get the same confidence.
- Study low-level systems: networking, computer architecture, semiconductors, chips, physics. Understanding the layers of abstraction underneath software is useful, and he calls "you don't need to study software engineering" nonsense.
- People who understand AI and software well are paid more than ever. Pay for software, electrical and industrial engineers in the Bay Area keeps rising.
- He regrets not making enough connections with smart people at school. He was very introverted and didn't stay in touch with the talented ones, and thinks he could have met his current co-founder there.
- Should you finish school? "Probably", if the degree gets tested by nature or free markets, meaning feedback from reality (building something that works, compiling code that executes, selling something people buy).
- He is skeptical of degrees where feedback comes mainly from graders or award committees, such as social sciences. He calls this "not real" and says you may only be having a good time.
- He recommends engineering for the students there and says to consider switching if you aren't studying it.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Naval contrasts entrepreneur and investor temperaments, and says the one lesson every veteran repeats is that it's the people. He covers partner selection (intelligence, energy, integrity), why consumer web winners need Silicon Valley, how to approach busy buyers, and why angels only fund companies with large-exit potential.

chunks.heading: Entrepreneur vs. investor temperament
chunks.text:
Naval says entrepreneurs and investors need very different emotional temperaments. He has done both.

**Entrepreneur**
- Passionate, "almost irrationally optimistic," and highly committed to the single thing they are focused on.
- Has to "break down doors and pull trains and do whatever it takes" to get people to follow the vision.
- Needs focus and wants fairly constant feedback from the environment.

**Investor (angel or VC)**
- A little cynical, a little pessimistic, rational, and constantly re-evaluating each opportunity. All day long passionate entrepreneurs are selling to them.
- Must context switch very quickly across many different things.
- Must stay dispassionate. People call investors with bad news, not good news, and the investor has to work through it without it ruining their day.
- Feedback cycles are very slow. "You find out 10 years later if you were any good at what you're doing or not."

His background at the time (2010):
- Founded epinions.com (went public as part of shopping.com) and vast.com, a white-label classified service that powers parts of AOL, Kelley Blue Book, Vehix and Yahoo Travel.
- Co-author of Venture Hacks and launched AngelList.
- Runs a small fund with dozens of investments, including Twitter, Disqus, DocVerse, Mixer Labs and Social Gold.

chunks.heading: "It's the people, stupid": pick partners on intelligence, energy and integrity
chunks.text:
Naval says the advice he ignored early on was the one every veteran gives. It holds in any business, whether the speaker is Warren Buffett on public investing, an experienced VC on private investing, or an older entrepreneur on starting a company. All of them say "it's the people, stupid." People nod, but he says you only understand it about 10 years later, "once you've worked with enough of the wrong people."

His rule is to find a great partner, whatever you are doing, and look for all three of these:
- Very high intelligence.
- Very high energy.
- Very high integrity.

"You can't compromise on any one of them." The failure modes are:
- A partner who isn't smart does you no good.
- A partner who isn't hard working does you no good.
- The worst case is "a smart hard working crook who ends up working against your interests."

Integrity takes a lot of time spent with someone to judge.

He also says most companies fail. That does not always mean falling apart. Many fail to execute, fail to deliver, or fail to realize their full potential. The cause is interpersonal conflict, either between founders or between a founder and an investor. "At the end of the day, it's people issues, which is surprising and ironic."

chunks.heading: Why consumer web founders should be in Silicon Valley
chunks.text:
Naval started in Boston and found it hard to build a technology company there. Boston's definition of technology was "a little more backwards-looking." He moved to Silicon Valley.

Obvious reasons:
- Universities are there.
- Other tech entrepreneurs are there.
- Investors are there, so raising money is easier.

Non-obvious reasons:
- Partners are there, and most networking and partnerships "happen serendipitously, not by design."
- People use the latest gadgets, so you can see what will be mainstream a year or two out.
- "It's in the air, it's in the water."

Evidence from his own experience: at Vast he built a team of 100 people overseas. It was a great team, but it "took us a year longer and we lost a lot of time doing it."

Why it matters most for consumer web:
- Consumer web businesses are mostly winner-take-all. "There's only room for one Twitter and one Facebook and one eBay and one Google," and second place loses big.
- So founders need every advantage. Silicon Valley may be one item on a checklist of 10, "but if you want to win, it needs all 10."
- He grants that you can succeed elsewhere. He names a thriving New York scene, a smaller one in Boston, and opportunity in Seattle and Austin.
- He still expects that when a company gets big and "goes for the gold," it will probably move to Silicon Valley.

chunks.heading: How investors evaluate founders: the product is a resume
chunks.text:
- When an entrepreneur shows a product, Naval is "evaluating it as a resume for the person." He asks what they are capable of.
- He wants to see how much they have done, not how much they talk.
- Silicon Valley, like Hollywood or New York, is a magnet place that attracts many good talkers. To separate talkers from doers, look at what they have built and how much they accomplished with very few resources.
- On the people side, he spends time with them and asks four things:
  - Are they good people?
  - Do they work really hard?
  - Are they very smart and thoughtful?
  - Can they accomplish things on their own?

chunks.heading: How to pitch busy investors (or any large buyer)
chunks.text:
Naval says investor time is "assaulted from all directions." The same is true of any buy-side role, such as a buyer at a Fortune 500 company who gets sales calls all day. The same techniques apply to any large buyer. The principle is to respect their time as much as you respect your own.

Tactics:
- Don't insist on in-person meetings.
- Qualify the leads first.
- Send something in writing first.
- Get a very good introduction from someone trusted.
- Don't browbeat them into an in-person meeting or a call.
- Let them screen first via text, a summary or a business plan.
- If they ask for it, follow up with an in-person meeting.

chunks.heading: Secrecy: ideas are not worth hiding
chunks.text:
- First-timers are "too secretive." Experienced founders "don't care."
- After a few companies, you see how much execution difficulty and risk there is, and how hard it is to get people to listen and believe you.
- Eventually founders "shout your idea from the rooftops just in the hope that somebody will actually use the product." The problem flips to getting anyone to pay attention.
- If an idea would lose all its value once someone else figures it out, "it's not something you can execute on as a business. It's not a real idea."

chunks.heading: Why angels won't fund small or niche ideas
chunks.text:
Naval calls this a large misconception that disserves entrepreneurs. Many founders think they can carve out a small niche with little competition, aim for a $20 or 30 million exit, and raise angel money on that basis.

His reasoning:
- He cites Keynes's "beauty contest." An investor is betting on the company most likely to be selected in the next round, not the most beautiful company.
- The real risk is that the company runs out of money. "Every company needs more money than it thought it did," so future financing risk is high.
- VCs only fund companies with potential large exits.
- Because of that, angels will only fund companies with potential large exits. Otherwise they risk funding a company that no VC will touch later.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Naval talks with Scott Adams about what drives success: hard work matters less than judgment in an age of infinite leverage, general intelligence plus open-mindedness is the meta-skill, and early-stage investing is about the entrepreneur. He also covers blockchains as a new form of network governance, Bitcoin as insurance against politicians, and cooperation as the human advantage.

chunks.heading: Success factors: how Naval rates hard work, network, intelligence and skills
chunks.text:
Scott Adams asked Naval to score success variables from 1 to 10.

- **Hard work:** "3 or 4 maybe," and about 7 or 8 at some point early on.
  - Silicon Valley winner-take-all races (the next $50 billion company) are the exception. Only one company can win, so everything scores 10.
  - For most people the reason is leverage: "technology capital media make it so easy to multiply your work."
  - What you do and how well you do it matters more than how hard you do it.
- **Network:** Early on it didn't feel important to him. Looking back, he rates it about 8 or 9.
  - Moving to Silicon Valley was a network decision, because you join the network by moving there.
  - His college network mattered little. He built work that people would see and recognize, and the network emerged from that.
  - Where you start out means fewer hops to where you want to end up.
- **Intelligence:** He calls himself biased and rates general intelligence as the number one trait.
  - Pair it with open-mindedness and intellectual curiosity.
  - A smart, open-minded person who questions everything will work out the rest at a good enough level. That includes nutrition, workouts, habits, making money, sales and persuasion, and development skills.
  - He calls this "the meta thing" that makes you pretty good at everything.
- **Skills:** He agrees that the right combination of skills matters (the "skill stack" idea Scott raised).

chunks.heading: Backing entrepreneurs versus businesses
chunks.text:
- **Entrepreneurs:** Many businesses fail, and good entrepreneurs chasing bad businesses fail too. But the entrepreneurs themselves don't fail over a long enough period.
  - "When you meet the right entrepreneur you know they're gonna be a winner." The open question is how many attempts it takes.
  - His implication for investors is to back the person a few times.
- **Early stage versus mature:** Early on it is much more about the people.
  - As a business gets larger and more mature it becomes "like a fortress," and the business matters more than the operator.
- **Buffett's approach:** Buffett says to invest in businesses any idiot could run, because one eventually will.
  - Naval says Buffett invests in natural monopolies (moats).
  - His Coca-Cola example is physiological and psychological addiction. Cola has "zero taste build-up," so a heavy drinker never tires of it and can swap out water entirely.
  - He says products that go in your mouth form deep bonds, and he compares Coke to toothpaste and Gillette.
  - His point is that if your business is not a natural monopoly, then "it's all about the people."
- **Packaging as delight:** Amazon replaced cold packs with water bottles in its food delivery. A cold pack annoys the customer, but a free bottle feels like an extra. He compares this to Apple's packaging, where you fall in love before you touch the product.

chunks.heading: How Naval got started: Stuyvesant and the network effect of a credential
chunks.text:
- He was an unknown kid in New York City from an immigrant, single-parent household. He wasn't a good student.
- Passing the Stuyvesant High School entrance test, an SAT-style exam taken in eighth grade, "saved my life."
  - Stuyvesant was the hardest public school in New York City to get into. Bronx Science and Brooklyn Tech took the next-highest scorers.
  - The school brand opened the door to an Ivy League college and then to tech.
- He says it started with no network but quickly became a network, and that a test-based credential gave an instant validation network.
- His first tech startup was in the dot-com boom. His team treated hard work as heroic and competed to spend time at the office. They slept under their desks and ate the packing foam from Amazon shipments.
  - He frames this as young founders not knowing better.
  - It fits his current view that how hard you work matters less than what you work on.

chunks.heading: Blockchain as a new form of network governance
chunks.text:
- **Core framing:** Humans win as cooperators. English, the US, the dollar and Uber are all networks.
  - Humans can cooperate across genetic boundaries, unlike ants or bees.
  - Every network needs control over cheaters: who gets in, who gets paid, who pays, and who is not doing their job.
- **Four historical governance forms:** individual rulers (kings, tyrants, emperors), elites or aristocracies, democracies ("mobs"), and companies such as Uber or Facebook.
- **The fifth form:** Blockchains bring market-style governance. It is code running in the cloud that nobody owns.
  - Example: a storage network where anyone who contributes storage gets paid and anyone who uses it pays.
  - The blockchain is the ledger of debits and credits. It punishes cheaters and rewards reliable contributors.
- **Permissionless, programmable, uncensorable networks:**
  - Today you must go through Visa, MasterCard or PayPal to move money in code. That means big fees, no micro-transactions and permission requirements.
  - Finance has been shielded from programmers. Programmable finance lets engineers take over a privilege held by bankers, which is the "money craze."
  - Uncensorable means no gatekeeper in the middle taking 30%, and no shutdown of access in places where Twitter or Facebook are blocked.
- **Uses beyond money:** energy grids and bandwidth allocation.

chunks.heading: Why Bitcoin is hard for governments to stop
chunks.text:
- Bitcoin "is basically insurance against politicians." It has value only because it isn't politically controlled.
  - A cryptocurrency controlled by a dictator, a democracy, a mob, an elite or a company is "an oxymoron" and has no value.
  - The US dollar already offers a government-backed option, so a government coin offers nothing new.
- **Legal angle:** Code is speech, and the First Amendment protects it. He points to the Clipper Chip and PGP export fights under Clinton. He also cites 3D-printed gun schematics (Cody Wilson, Defense Distributed) as not illegal.
- **Technical angle against a ban:**
  - Crypto traffic can be hidden inside other traffic.
  - Other traffic will eventually hide inside crypto traffic.
  - Blockchains can be synced by satellite broadcast. A hidden computer in a remote area could validate for its community.
- **Market view:** He says all the Bitcoin in the world was then worth about one twentieth of gold. He reads that as the market pricing a low probability that it survives. He says that if it survives it will go "20 X from here."
- He declines to give investment advice and says to do your own homework.

chunks.heading: Reproducing ideas, and the Golden Age view
chunks.text:
- **Ideas as reproduction:** He says having an impact can matter more than having kids. He suggests that "memetic replication is more effective than pure genetic replication." Scott's books and his own writing are the example.
- **Golden Age:** He agrees with Scott's definition. Things are moving the right way on the big issues, and the remaining problems are psychological rather than resource problems.
  - Technology and capitalism have created abundance. Infant mortality and poverty are falling, and diseases such as malaria are being eradicated.
  - Progress is unevenly distributed. The faster it happens, the more extreme the gaps. China has both billionaires and people on a dollar a day.
  - He says perception that things are getting worse persists even though the statistics are improving.
  - Prosperity continues "as long as we don't blow up the engines that create it, which are basically capitalism, technology and trade."

chunks.heading: Cooperation, opponents and what to teach
chunks.text:
- **Cooperation:** "Cooperation is the human advantage." Anytime you can cooperate with more people, you win.
  - This is why people move to Silicon Valley for tech or Hollywood for acting. You connect with like-minded people in one ecosystem.
  - The more people you can work with, the richer you will be.
- **Opponents:** His first step is not declaring anyone your opponent. Often the people we call enemies don't see us that way, and as ego softens we see they never were.
  - He argues it is better to assume you have no enemies. Two companies that find a way to work together are probably better off.
- **Teaching (his curriculum):**
  - Math and applied science, taught through building and experiments. He says all high-value advancement comes from technology, which is applied science and applied math.
  - Reading and writing, plus persuasion.
  - Nutrition by logging what you eat and seeing what works for you, rather than dogma.
  - Fitness by finding a sport you love and learning the basics.
  - Basic programming and how hardware and chips work.
  - Strategy. He learned it from strategy war games as a kid, and he maps business and politics onto them. He says he has barely read game theory books.
  - History, geography and literature should be left to reading in spare time. Forced reading makes kids hate it.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Naval explains how collapsing startup costs are dislocating venture, why proprietary deal flow is dead, and why compounding long-term relationships beat over-optimizing each deal. He also covers AngelList's platform strategy (never charge startups), how his team passed the JOBS Act by acting like a startup, and why networking is overrated.

chunks.heading: Naval on how the cost of starting a company collapsed
chunks.text:
- Naval argues the thing that disrupted venture capital was "the cost of building a business has collapsed," not Angelist or Y Combinator (he credits YC for pioneering the new incubator model).
- His 1999 company Opinions raised $8 million in its first round. It took 6 months to ship the website. The team bought its own Sun servers and Oracle databases, hosted them in its own office, and paid for a T1 line. There was no MySQL, no Git, and no data centers.
- Today the same work is rented:
  - AWS for hosting.
  - Google for acquiring customers.
  - Twitter for customer service.
  - Facebook for marketing.
  - Heroku for deployment.
  - Elance or oDesk for part-time labor.
  - Mechanical Turk for cleanup tasks.
  - Kickstarter or Angelist for money.
- He says "a single person with a lever can truly move the earth." Great businesses can be "built entirely through leverage," talking to the world through APIs with very little headcount.
- He thinks Instagram is not an aberration and expects "a lot more Instagrams." He disagrees with Marc Andreessen that Instagram needed 200 people to monetize; he says five more people would have been enough.
- Seed rounds are mostly $750K to $1M, but many companies can get far on $250K. Incubators prototype and test for $25K in 3 months, and "that's the competition."
- Consequence for hiring: before product-market fit, employees are really "late founders." They can start their own company or join an incubator, so the old pattern of raising $1M and giving the first engineer a quarter point no longer works.
- Consequence for VCs: the first-check role moved from Sand Hill Road to super angels around 2007, then to incubators. Companies now brand themselves as "YC backed" or "Techstars backed," not as a Sequoia company. That pushes VCs further back in the feeder chain, which is dangerous because brands are built by forming early relationships with entrepreneurs.

chunks.heading: Company size shrinking and the future of work
chunks.text:
- Naval's contrarian belief: the efficient size of a company is "shrinking very rapidly." The industrial revolution created economies of scale that pushed people into factories of 5,000 to 10,000. Information technology has reversed that.
- He expects many small companies loosely coupled through APIs and processes, and more contract and gig work. People will take a job for 2 or 3 days, get rated, then take the next. "In the future we're all Uber drivers."
- He expects more billion-dollar businesses built by four or five people. The VC industry still believes you must put a couple hundred million into a company to scale, and he thinks that is wrong.
- Pieces that look non-outsourceable today will be outsourced: sales, revenue collection, bookkeeping reconciliation, and the early stage of hiring.
- He says any good entrepreneur could build Facebook's feature set today with a few hundred people. Large founders know 80% of staff aren't needed but can't tell which 80%.
- Productivity gap: people comfortable with information technology have a "10x advantage in productivity or greater." He says "the smart are getting richer" and society doesn't know how to handle it.
- His definition of work: "a set of things you have to do that you don't want to do." If you want to do it, it isn't work. Startups feel harder but are done "your way."
- On Yahoo, he says it needs to exit entire businesses and focus. "Betting on mobile" is too broad; you have to pick which part of mobile.

chunks.heading: Seed economics, experiments, and failing fast
chunks.text:
- Naval says the seed-to-Series-A crunch is mostly a pricing and expectations problem. Many seed companies are "cheap, low-cost experiments" and should be treated as such.
- Prices must reflect a hit rate of 1 in 5 or 1 in 10, not 1 in 3. In his day, a company that raised its first few million had a 1-in-2 or 1-in-3 chance of reaching the next round. Today a seed company has about a 1-in-10 chance of reaching a Series A.
- Early investors who forget it's an experiment may push you to raise a "seed prime" or a premature Series A. He says that traps you "like Sisyphus," pushing a rock uphill when there may be no market or no right team.
- Advice: "if you're going to fail, fail fast." Acknowledge reality, then try again, as YC companies that go back into YC do.
- He thinks the soft-landing acqui-hire is overrated by press coverage because failed companies stay quiet. Few companies get one. Acquirers separate investors from talent by paying retention and earn-out to the team, so investors often lose money.
- Investors who add multiples on acquisitions to term sheets have no real leverage. The acquirer can offer 10 cents on the dollar, and the company's alternative is zero.
- Not every company should be funded. He doesn't want unfundable companies funded, because many good businesses are ruined by funding: expectations rise and they "have to do stupid things to generate return."
- Lifestyle businesses are a put-down from the investor side. He says everyone would love one: you set your hours, keep the profits, and aren't up at night trying to turn it into a billion-dollar business.
- Timing and luck matter. A photo app with a dozen predecessors and a dozen successors won only because of timing (pre- or post-iPhone). Opinions (1999) couldn't become Yelp because too few local businesses and users were online.
- Network effects need density. Social networks failed in 1999 because not enough of your friends were online. Naval says path and product outcomes are hard to predict, and Twitter turned out differently than its founders intended.

chunks.heading: Raising money: terms, relationships, and choosing investors
chunks.text:
- Naval says term sheets were a "black art." Investors see 10 to 20 a year and have institutional memory. A founder negotiating a first term sheet knows nothing, and the lawyers get more business from VCs than from founders.
- Old-style traps he lists:
  - Liquidation preference multiples, or getting paid back and also participating in the upside.
  - Anti-dilution handling of down rounds.
  - Board control and who can fire the CEO.
  - Investors pushing out the founder, installing a friendly CEO, then recapping in a down round until they own all the equity.
- His Venture Hacks blog explained the game theory of term sheets and led to Angelist. Terms are now far more standardized and often founder-friendly (convertible notes, founders with strong voting control).
- Contracts are negotiated for the worst case, not the best case. Game theory "boils down to power; there is no concept of fairness." Use power to get a fair outcome, or at least know the consequences if you lack it.
- Founders can overreach too. He cites uncapped notes and sees notes that cap conversion but return only the money if the company sells for a lot.
- Negotiation rule of thumb: "negotiate hard, get what you're fairly due, and at the end give something back." Money has karma. Strong hand means a strong outcome is deserved, but leave something on the table.
- Compound interest: "all the returns in life come from compound interest," meaning the length and strength of relationships. Examples: the PayPal mafia, marriage, Warren Buffett.
- Spotting short-term players: ask whether you like them, whether you trust them, and whether you'll be doing business with them in a decade. Check references and how considered they are. Trust shows once "the money hits the table."
- He has dropped investments because a founder fought for a tiny piece, which signaled over-optimizing for the moment.
- Iterated prisoner's dilemma: cooperation pays when you'll play again. Newcomers in a hot market are tempted to cheat for a $20M to $50M win. He says people with the wrong motives win "probably more than half the time," but you only have to get it right once.
- On choosing investors: "go for whoever trusts you, likes you and will support you over who you think is going to add value." Value-add is now available from many places. Good advisers are cheap; he asks whether you'd pay $2M in valuation for it, when advisers can be paid in stock.
- Brand reflects how nice a VC is once they have control. If you raise a lot, you will lose board control, and if you hit a hiccup you must get a bridge from insiders.
- Mix and match instead of one bundle: advice and network from the incubator, a first big bet from a prolific seed investor, then one or two angels as sherpas or board members. That gives you a counterweight when the VC arrives. He notes incubators "unionized" entrepreneurs.
- He estimates one founder spends about half their time over the company's life on investor issues: pitching, keeping them happy, searching for the next one, or negotiating.
- Online fundraising is more objective than offline. Investors judge metrics, product quality, who else is in the round (social proof), and famous advisers. If you can only tell instead of show, it works less well. If you can show, you reach thousands of investors at once and can run a competitive round.

chunks.heading: How Angelist evolved and its Craigslist model
chunks.text:
- Naval says the vision evolved daily. They started with fundraising intros, then tried Series A (done dozens of times but a higher bar and relationship business), then small business equity (failed because there are few angels outside tech), then going global (only works in a few towns; China is a black box).
- The model is Craigslist: connect people to services, "charge for very, very few of them," and keep it seamless and no-hassle. The name was no accident.
- Talent product: launched a couple of months before this talk and "quite a bit bigger" than fundraising by volume. About 300 startup-investor intros last week, and roughly three times that in talent. 2,000 startups are recruiting (Quora, Kickstarter, Path, Khan Academy, Pocket, Climate Corp, Yelp). About 250 vetted candidates are added each week. Spread mainly by word of mouth plus one email to the existing user base.
- Talent rules: no recruiters, transparency on equity and salary ranges (companies that refused were removed), and candidates talk to a founder or senior person, not an HR screen. Recruiters charge $25K to $30K per placement. Angelist paid one $25K to build the system that routes around recruiters. It didn't charge yet and planned a model where small companies could pay in equity or notes, far below market.
- Pricing principles:
  - Never charge startups and investors for meeting each other, to avoid adverse selection.
  - Never knowingly screw over startups ("don't be evil").
  - Startups can't pay, so find someone else in the ecosystem who will: big companies recruiting, jobs and real estate analogues, vendors who want to reach startups at funding time (such as payments companies), and out-of-market capital.
  - Investor fees of "$1,000 a year" are "not even worth it."
- Network is an information good: "doesn't cost much to give away." Naval plans to make it widely available and charge cost-plus, far below other options. Services embedded include lawyers, press, M&A groups (over 30 actively use it, including Square, Yahoo, Google, Groupon), PR, back office, and early customers.
- Docs: free closings on Series Seed docs (Ted Wang's), with law firms such as Wilson Sonsini and Cooley doing the closing online for free. It was a loss leader for them. Cost came from negotiation over pet clauses. Online, changes cost $20,000, so social pressure standardizes. Standardized docs removed "expensive lawyers" and weeks of negotiation.
- Incubator integration: sent 500 Startups 600 companies in two weeks with structured, ranked data. Plans for Angel Pad and Techstars Boston the next day and dozens of incubators by Q1. Some VC funds use it to find initial $100K seed checks. All processing queues are open to everyone, with no preferential access.
- Adverse-selection rebuttal: Uber, Pinterest, Branch, Rally, Kaggle, Recurly, and Flashsoft were on Angelist. About 2,000 companies on the done-deals page raised over $1.3B trailing, probably closer to $2B. Out-of-market VCs (such as a Brussels VC with three deals) say they wouldn't be in business without it. One company chose a London term sheet over a local one.
- VC friendliness: top-tier VCs like it best because they are the bottleneck and it lets them view more deals efficiently. They have embedded associates who sit in on Tuesday queue reviews.

chunks.heading: Deal flow, access, and what investors actually fund
chunks.text:
- Naval says "proprietary deal flow is dead." In 2007 about 90% was proprietary and closed; he estimated under 50% and falling. Drivers: lower capital needs, platforms like Angelist and YC, and the ability to launch a product first and raise later, so there is less to hide.
- Founders who stay proprietary "are self-limiting the market for their shares." Older entrepreneurs do this; younger ones know it's open and transparent. There are dozens (maybe over 100) of great VC firms and thousands of great angels you can't reach by knocking on doors.
- What VCs still have is proprietary access: the ability to win a hot deal. That comes from brand, access, and know-how. Top brands such as Andreessen or Sequoia can outmuscle anyone. New brands (super angels, Google Ventures, Yuri Milner, YC, True Ventures, SV Angel) were mostly built on being entrepreneur-friendly.
- Example: SV Angel let a founder keep the last $75,000 in a shutting-down company so he could ride out until his next job.
- Super angel definition: willing to write small checks, decide quickly, and forgo normal control terms such as a board seat. He sees them becoming the next branded Series A firms, with seed extensions that look like old Series A amounts.
- Investor-facing advice: what investors fund is teams, so fill out team bios. The four things investors look at: traction, a unique product, a stellar team, or social proof. Listing early has no downside, but with 100,000 profiles you won't get noticed without something spectacular or a promotion.
- Social proof: someone worth listening to commits their time (adviser, key hire like a Rails core contributor) or money.
- Traction: "quantitative evidence of customer demand." Enterprise: two or three paying early customers. Consumer: possibly hundreds of thousands of users. Mobile: download rate. The bar is a moving target. Naval's examples: two years earlier a daily-deals startup funded pre-traction; 18 months earlier none funded at any traction; 12 months earlier a mobile app with 10,000 downloads funded, but now it takes a few hundred thousand and rapid adoption. Use trending, featured, and done-deals lists to see the current bar.
- Incubators outside hubs are hard because funding markets develop backwards (public markets first, then late stage, then earlier). Naval says some incubators, such as Startmate (Australia) and Founder Fuel (Montreal), skim top local talent and bridge them to US investors.

chunks.heading: YC's model and how Naval ran the Jobs Act campaign
chunks.text:
- Why YC worked, per Naval:
  - Paul Graham's reach and writing pulled in talent that otherwise had no path into Silicon Valley.
  - It took a much smaller stake than older idea-lab models (which took 30 to 40%) and the company, not the incubator, had the idea.
  - It overlaid a college template: roughly a 3-month semester, a project to ship, weekly meetings, office hours, and a demo day.
  - Economics are great with minimal capital: a hit like Dropbox is enough, and the founder doesn't need to raise from LPs repeatedly. It overturned the VC rule that more money raised means more made.
- Other incubators are specializing (Angel Pad for ex-Googlers, Lemnos for hardware) and by geography. He expects "MITs and Caltechs" next to YC.
- Jobs Act (securities law) campaign:
  - Securities laws date from 1934. Much of what happens at demo days was technically illegal. Angelist could not offer docs without being a broker-dealer.
  - They hired "gumshoe lobbyists" on a contingency success fee, found through friends and Twitter. He says "all the lobbyist can do is open a door; you still have to make the pitch."
  - The pitch to Congress: Angelist was spreading investment around the country in every state, so they could show investors and startups in each district willing to stand up.
  - He spent about 6 months calling in favors: calling congressmen, telling them about raising or investing through Angelist. He estimated about 100 favors, and a random five came together. He started believing there was a 10% chance of success and judged expected value worth it.
  - Approach it like a startup: success fees, and when told a Word-document petition was enough, they built a viral Twitter petition in a 36-hour all-nighter. It had login with Angelist or Twitter, photos and bios, and got 5,000 signatures from investors and entrepreneurs, sliced by location, influence, investments, and senator. A union petition had 3,600. The data could say "I see that guy; he's one of your big campaign donors."
  - Branding: the bill was a bundle named the "Jobs Act." "What congressperson can vote against something called the Jobs Act?" He advises rebranding immigration reform; mixing skilled and unskilled is "the wrong brand."
- Securities law warnings: don't get ahead of securities law. Raising from unaccredited investors or handling money through an unlicensed broker-dealer can void the entire transaction, give investors rescission rights, and carry personal liability. Uber, Lyft, and Airbnb can route around local laws because local rules are easier to change once people are galvanized. Securities laws are "radioactive." The right order is to get the law changed first, then act.
- Crowdfunding experiment: small-dollar online investments via SecondMarket (a registered broker-dealer), accredited investors only, with suitability and Patriot Act checks. He called it a test.

chunks.heading: Saying no, meetings, and networking
chunks.text:
- Naval's "mediocre superpower": saying no without feeling guilty. Most startups aren't ready to be funded, can't all be met, and require triage.
- Meeting policy: he owns the domain idontdocoffee.com. The ladder is email first (so you can help 30 companies instead of one), then phone, then Skype, then a meeting, bundling meetings (four in an hour) and staying efficient. He cites Harj Taggar of YC: shortening office hours made them more efficient, because there's no time for pleasantries.
- Advice to startups: avoid meetings unless necessary. "Networking is overrated." Instead, "go do something great and your network will instantly emerge." With a great product or customer base he said "we will get you funded." Meet people to recruit or learn from smart people, but only if you have something to offer.
- Lawyers: the best act as cheap advisers, and he urges founders to seek founder-friendly ones. Names he gave: Buddy Arnheim (Perkins Coie), Jorge del Calvo (Pillsbury), Eric Benisek (Venture Law Group), and Silicon Legal Strategy. He notes lawyers must brand and prove their value more than investors, since investors can "write you a check." He thinks no startup could operate if it followed every law, but you still need a lawyer.
- On patents: he hasn't been hit by patent trolls. He suggests the bar of "obvious to those skilled in the art" be enforced, software and business-model patents be removed or held to a higher bar, terms be shortened from 17 years, and an open expert-panel review be used.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Taleb lectures on skin in the game, then Naval interviews him. Naval's own contributions apply the ideas to startups: judge engineers by output, distrust polished pitches, discount macro and conferences, treat courage as the unfakeable virtue, and stay in the game to survive.

chunks.heading: Judge by reality, not by peers
chunks.text:
- Naval agrees with Taleb that people judged only by peers drift away from reality. Examples are academics and journalists.
- Tech has the same problem. Companies track inputs (hours, being in at 8:00 a.m., 40-50 hour weeks) instead of outputs.
- He argues a great engineer can create a billion dollars of value, and a bad one can destroy value. Neither outcome depends on hours put in.
- Satoshi Nakamoto is his example of that scale of output.
- In markets, put your money where your mouth is. Online arguments about Bitcoin's price are pointless when you can short it or take a position on an exchange.
- Experts who called Bitcoin "rat poison" or a Ponzi at low prices were wrong while it kept rising. Without a P&L they pay nothing for being wrong.

chunks.heading: Macro is a distraction; polish is a poor signal when investing
chunks.text:
- Naval says he got an economics degree alongside his computer science degree and calls it a mistake. In 20 years of venture investing, "macro has been completely worthless" to him.
- He calls macro entertainment and "another branch of politics". He says even micro isn't judged by contact with reality.
- On early-stage teams, he avoids founders who look incredibly polished: good PowerPoint, well dressed, presents well.
- He prefers the person busy at the computer who gets flustered at the whiteboard and over-explains, but has real substance.
- He goes further and argues against business plans. Plans are too well written and full of buzzwords, and rejecting them on that basis is reasonable.
- Awards like "VC of the year" or "angel of the year" are nonsense to him. The reward is making the money, like simply owning the Bitcoin.

chunks.heading: Asymmetry, optionality and anti-fragility in crypto
chunks.text:
- Naval describes Bitcoin as an asymmetric bet. If you lose, you lose your money. If it becomes digital gold, you could make 50x or 100x.
- He calls it anti-fragile. Each hack, attack or ecosystem failure it survives gets fixed by developers, so the system improves and is better prepared for the next shock.
- He treats shorting crypto as the wrong side of the trade: a concave position with limited upside and large downside. His example is shorting at $40 and watching it run 100x.
- He notes trial and error is a main source of asymmetry, because you keep what works and discard what doesn't.
- Competition between cryptocurrencies makes them anti-fragile, as competition between issuers did in ancient times. People pick the currency least likely to be debased.
- He sees crypto as an attempt to separate money from the state, like separating church and state. If it works, he expects it to be just as impactful and to take a long time.

chunks.heading: Lindy and what survives
chunks.text:
- Naval defines Lindy as stands the test of time. A book that has lasted thousands of years is likely to last thousands more, and survival so far is the best predictor of survival.
- Applied to technology, new things are more vulnerable to newer things. He treats old tools such as the fork as the model for what lasts.
- A commercial transaction coupled with a financial one is a Lindy concept, and blockchain inherits it.
- Bitcoin is the most Lindy cryptocurrency because it has survived longest.
- He says it won't be digital gold until it has survived long enough. The longer it survives, the more faith and money people can put into it.

chunks.heading: Minority rule and intransigence
chunks.text:
- Naval calls the minority rule counterintuitive and says it changed how he thinks about many things. The idea is that a small intransigent minority can set the rules for a flexible majority.
- He first hoped the most outraged people on Twitter, on the extreme left, the extreme right or in crypto, were simply ineffective and off in a corner. The minority rule shows that if they are intransigent enough, they can control society.
- In elections he rejects the view that the median voter decides. If a few percent of voters won't compromise, for example Bernie voters who refuse the mainstream Democrat or hard-right voters who refuse Jeb Bush, candidates must appeal to them.
- He compares revolutionaries: small bands who won't tolerate the status quo, while most people in the middle just go along.
- For crypto, he imagines 10-20% of good Silicon Valley developers refusing any pay except crypto. Payroll systems would then switch to offering it.
- He says this lesson applies when you tolerate intolerance: "you're going to live with the consequences".

chunks.heading: Science, survival and dynamic risk
chunks.text:
- Naval states that science can only disprove, not prove. "Proven by science" misreads the process.
- He says the result isn't what matters; the process is. Consensus and counts of Nobel winners don't matter, because one counterexample can destroy an argument.
- On path dependence, he explains with Russian roulette. Six people each playing once for a billion dollars is very different from one person playing six times in sequence. Confusing the two gives the wrong answer.
- Loss aversion, he argues, is rational, because if you go bust you can never recover. In crypto, going all-short or selling everything can take you out of the game for good.
- His rule is to "stay in the game".

chunks.heading: Courage, skin in the game and conferences
chunks.text:
- Naval says courage is the one virtue that cannot be faked. On Twitter you can fake other virtues, but not taking on someone powerful under your own name rather than a troll account.
- He credits Taleb with naming the "intellectual yet idiot" and the Bob Rubin trade by name. In his view Taleb's work will last a thousand years.
- He offers a test for any proposed censorship mechanism: build it, then hand it to your enemy to run. If you're unwilling, you just want to be in charge.
- He distinguishes equality of opportunity from equality of outcome. Equality of outcome is communism and coercion, while equality of opportunity is what you strive for, narrowed through education.
- He generally doesn't travel for conferences, because they lean toward signaling, like looking busy for your boss. Sitting in an audience has little value when you could watch it on YouTube.
- The exception is meeting the right people when they are small.
- He recommends reading Taleb's five Incerto books, including Skin in the Game, Black Swan and Antifragile, instead of reading anything else that year.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Naval gives his latest thinking on happiness as a personal skill. Happiness and the self are just thoughts, chronic unhappiness is an ego trip, and peace comes from few chosen desires, thin identity and truth. He frames life as health, wealth, truth, love and beauty, pursued in seasons, with high agency over your whole life, not just your work.

chunks.heading: Happiness as a skill, and why Naval doesn't chase it
chunks.text:
- Naval says happiness is "a highly personal skill" and that his "latest thinking" is that there's "no such thing as happiness". It is a construct of the mind, a thought that comes and goes.
- He says he cares more about peace and being okay with things as they are. He frames this as his own exploration ("I'm not an enlightened being"), subject to change.
- Happiness and unhappiness do not exist in the outside world. Events are impermanent and out of your control, and the world "can't make you any more unhappy than you let it."
- Exception: physical pain demands a response, which makes the mind unhappy.
- Desires should be few and consciously chosen.
- Higher motives help. If you work on something larger than yourself (a mission, children), it hurts less when outcomes go against you, because it isn't personal.
- His tweet: "the more you think about yourself, the less happy you're going to be."
- He recommends strategic indifference to problems outside your control, such as politics and distant wars.
- He doesn't want pure peace either. He says doing nothing gets boring, so he prefers to do what he does without overthinking it, "row, row, row your boat, gently down the stream."

chunks.heading: Meditation, self-observation and deconstructing emotion
chunks.text:
- Naval says meditation is not for getting enlightened or calming down. Its purpose is to become self-observant, so you catch your mind doing things against your long-term interest.
- When you catch it, he suggests asking:
  - Is this true?
  - Is this desire important?
  - Do I need to suffer over this?
  - Is it easier to reinterpret this or to deal with the underlying problem?
- In his own sessions, the first 20 minutes are chaotic. After that the mind calms, and 30 to 50 minutes in it goes blank and blissful.
- Deconstructing an emotion:
  - Notice the bodily sensation (for example, a hollowness in the chest). Often it isn't actually unpleasant.
  - Notice the thought attached to it. Thoughts can't feel pain.
  - Ask who is labelling it unpleasant. That is just another thought.
- During one very unhappy period, part of him watched the unhappy part and saw it as an act "to feel important", with nothing actually being attacked.
- He credits no single silver bullet. His stress relief came from reading (Krishnamurti, Osho), some psychedelics ("you get the message, you hang up the phone"), meditation, introspection and thinking.
- He says no mental technique from someone else's mind works reliably. The right idea can change you instantly, while the wrong practice done for 30 years won't.

chunks.heading: Stay healthy, get wealthy, seek truth, give love, create beauty
chunks.text:
- Naval's framework: stay healthy, get wealthy, seek truth, give love, create beauty.
- Health is the baseline. "You're born healthy, you don't finish healthy."
- Wealth: "Money doesn't solve all your problems, but it solves all your money problems." Nobody wants less wealth.
- Truth:
  - He wants to know what is true and eliminate what is false, spiritually, scientifically, technologically and about human nature.
  - He says truth and love are the two things you'd take even if they made your life worse. He uses Neo versus Cipher in The Matrix: nobody wants to be Cipher.
  - His line: the closer you get to truth, the more silent you become inside.
- Love:
  - "It's better to be in love than to be loved." Being loved can feel clawing; being in love is the high.
  - Everyone needs something they love more than themselves, such as a mission, family, kids or religion.
- Beauty and creation:
  - Citing David Deutsch, he says humans are "universal explainers" meant to solve problems and advance knowledge.
  - Beautiful things are hard to vary, embody deep knowledge and make people want to use them.
  - He calls the iPhone "among the greatest works of art ever created": beautiful like jewelry, useful and knowledge-dense.
- He says to avoid cultivating unhappiness: "acute unhappiness is real or is useful but chronic unhappiness is an ego trip."

chunks.heading: Identity, depression and reinterpreting the past
chunks.text:
- Identity is what stands between you and reality. When something contradicts your identity, you fight it (his example: racism). Keep identity thin, because any chosen identity is a straitjacket.
- He cites psychologist William Glasser's choice theory: depression can be a series of childhood choices that became an unconscious, self-perpetuating habit, a way to get attention by hurting yourself.
- He accepts there are chemical components, but says "chemical imbalance" is too reductive an explanation. He says long-term drugs often cost you something fundamental.
- People can wrap an identity around being unhappy ("makes me special, interesting"), which makes it hard to undo.
- He is optimistic: there's no limit to how fast or how positively someone can change. "The most important thing with getting wealthy and being happy is just realize you can do it. It's your choice."
- Memories:
  - "You don't store memories of your past, you store interpretations of memories of your past."
  - Reinterpreting them is painful but useful, because it requires an ego hit (for example, admitting some of what went wrong was your own choices).
- Forgiveness is selfish in a useful way. Anger spikes cortisol, ages you and makes you miserable, so you forgive to clear your own mind.

chunks.heading: Order of pursuit: health, wealth, happiness, and seasons of life
chunks.text:
- His tweet: the three big ones are wealth, health and happiness. We pursue them in that order, but their importance is reversed.
- He holds the order loosely. Naturally happy people have the greatest gift. Health outranks wealth, per Confucius: "a healthy man wants 10,000 things, a sick man only wants one." He wouldn't give up any of the three.
- Wealth is best pursued young because of energy, flexibility, fewer obligations and optimism. It can be pursued later, but it's harder.
- His seasons of life:
  - Teens: learn and do.
  - 20s: work very hard "in the arena."
  - 30s: start harvesting, with contacts and energy.
  - 40s: harvest, watch health, and get happy "because there's not enough time left."
  - 50s: give back (philanthropy, civic contribution).
  - 60s: be a philosopher.
- Failure modes:
  - People overshoot wealth and sacrifice health and happiness.
  - Many wealthy contemporaries are unhappy and low agency outside work. He cites billionaires who won't travel because of school schedules or won't hire help, and who attend tedious obligatory events.
- Compounding: citing C.S. Lewis, small choices compound over decades into heaven or hell, so take responsibility for each one.
- Health: pain forces a quick feedback loop, so most people fix it eventually. He notes GLP-1 drugs are tackling obesity, the biggest mass-market driver of unhealthiness.

chunks.heading: Agency over your own life and the "lazy" 80/20
chunks.text:
- Naval says his life is "really good": at any time he is doing what he wants, nothing is obligatory, and if he isn't enjoying something he changes it fast.
- He wants the "fractal 80/20" in everything: the most output for the least effort across every area of life.
- "Lazy" means working on things that don't feel like work. Thinking about big questions feels less like work to him than not thinking about them.
- He'd rather learn from people who enjoy their lives (Osho, Steve Jobs) than from miserable truth-seekers like Schopenhauer.
- Jobs is his model of entrepreneurship because he was also an artist and a seeker, and tried to solve the big questions in life.
- Early-adopter note: he says his contribution on Twitter was being among the first, not unique.

chunks.heading: Relationships: no obligations, peers, and two happy people
chunks.text:
- Naval says he doesn't stay in relationships that make him unhappy. He fulfills duties to family, but not false ones.
- Every relationship besides blood ones is a value exchange, and needy relationships make you unhappy. "Neediness destroys a relationship or creates a fake relationship."
- He skips obligatory events (anniversaries, destination weddings, friends' birthdays unless fun). His rule is "no obligations", since obligations drive pain.
- His circle is people who are "similarly free, similarly low ego," who see each other voluntarily and don't take each other for granted. He invests in the relationships he values.
- Family: he has no estranged relatives, and the family functions well.
- "The secret to a happy relationship is two happy people." Happiness is personal. Telling someone to "cheer up" doesn't work, and putting relationships ahead of your own work and happiness means you "get neither".
- He wants peer relationships, even with employees, to avoid ritual and falseness.
- Parenting: he doesn't make his kids say thank you ("they're not an animal"). Genuine gratitude comes out on its own.
- On rituals:
  - He sees Valentine's Day, weddings and awards as forced ritual.
  - Genuine celebration is spontaneous.
  - He compares it to COVID breaking the commuting habit. If you don't feel like doing it naturally, fix the relationship or move on.

chunks.heading: Enlightenment, self-inquiry and "no self"
chunks.text:
- Naval says the self is "just a thought". Self-inquiry means looking for the "Eric" who suffers or feels pride. You can't pin it down, and the thoughts pointing at it die down once you see it isn't there.
- He says enlightened people have a persistent experience of no self. He treats it as binary rather than a path, and says it is not a state of perpetual happiness.
- Routes he mentions: some are natural, some have mystical experiences or psychotic breaks (he cites Krishnamurti's "process"), some meditate for decades, some devote their lives to service, and some use self-examination.
- Why it's now accessible: thanks to the internet, you can find living "enlightened" people on YouTube and Twitter. He has met close to a dozen and named Rupert Spira, Mooji, Nithyananda-style teachers, Steven Belcher, James Pierce, Effortless Stoicism, Kapil Gupta and Ascendor as examples.
- His test: spend enough time around them to see something genuinely bad happen, and watch for any perturbation. Another test: ask whether they'd be okay if they had never been enlightened. If the answer breaks, it was part of their identity.
- They still work, run companies, date and have desires, but without ego. He argues they may be more capable, since an enlightened "Terminator" is harder to beat than one wrapped in ego.
- On motivation: he says he hasn't met an enlightened person as motivated as him, but would take the trade of slightly less motivation for enlightenment.
- Happiness is a "strictly dominant strategy". No one chooses to go back to being poor or less happy, so "I don't value happiness" isn't true in practice. Chronic modern suffering often comes from feeling things chronically that were meant to be felt acutely.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Naval and Eric Jorgenson revisit Almanac ideas. Virtues are long-term selfishness, and a mission bigger than yourself pulls people in. Authenticity means dropping the mask. Life runs on exploring widely, then investing for compound returns. Judgment comes from deliberate iterations, not hours. Choose your environment and take inspiration over envy.

chunks.heading: Virtue as long-term selfishness, and avoiding cheap dopamine
chunks.text:
- Naval says "the modern devil is cheap dopamine." The seven deadly sins are all cheap dopamine: something that feels good now and screws you over later.
- He argues virtues are values that are good for you individually over a long enough time frame (long-term selfish). They also produce win-win outcomes for society, because they let people play iterated prisoner's dilemma and stag hunt games in a positive equilibrium.
- He calls a good life "the ultimate marshmallow test" (while noting the original experiment doesn't replicate).
- Modern traps he lists: politics, drugs, screen addiction and scrolling, porn, alcohol. On legalized weed, he says it "sucks the energy out of young men" and "you can't be ambitious if you're stoned all the time."
- He argues modern libertarianism took the wrong half: "free to do anything" became "celebrate anything," so everyone is a hedonist with no long-term stake, no shared ethos and no shared rules.
- He says atheism reaching the masses is a problem, because most people can't build their own operating system. Without a shared one you get anarchy or a state-imposed one, and he doubts the state's ethics beat the old religions'.
- On religion: "big religion causes a lot of problems but little religion is good." He favors village churches, broad unifying principles, and personally exploring the teachings of whichever religion resonates.

chunks.heading: Help locally first, and build a mission bigger than yourself
chunks.text:
- Naval prefers local charity (people down the street, people who work for you or with you) because it is practical, actionable and selfishly rewarding. Your money isn't wasted, tricked or redirected.
- He criticizes modern activism: "your family is broken, but you're going to fix the world." Agitating for distant causes you've never seen, while you can't fix local problems, is a disease. "You get the right to solve global problems after you solve local problems."
- Society gives more trust, leverage and influence to people who take care of those around them.
- On Elon Musk (before he was the richest man): when someone devotes their life to giving society what it needs, society has no choice but to give them what they want. You can't count that closely or do it purely for the payoff.
- A mission larger than yourself makes you a Schelling point (a rallying cry). "I want to make humans a spacefaring species" assembles builders who share that vision and now see a vehicle for it (SpaceX).
- The more universal the mission, the more people it pulls together, regardless of whether it is effective. He cites Martin Luther King's "I have a dream" speech and the appeal of Marxism.

chunks.heading: Ideas spread by spreadability, survive by correctness
chunks.text:
- Naval's version of the memetics point: an idea spreads according to its spreadability and survives according to its correctness.
- A civilization that adopts a bad idea because it spreads well can wipe itself off the map, as the Soviet Union did.
- Example: under Mao, the Great Leap Forward killed more Chinese people than all casualties of World War II (all nations combined, per Naval). China survived by adding a state-backed capitalist section: private farming, then private enterprises. "The more privatized they became, the faster they came up."
- Bad ideas get removed less by people learning than by the entities that hold them being eliminated. "Skin in the game will eliminate you." So you want to be an entity with correct ideas.
- His pseudo-spiritual take on David Deutsch: truth is a crystal in the multiverse. Falsehoods are infinitely variable, while true explanations are few and hard to vary, so the most truth-oriented versions of you are the most similar to each other.
- The goal is to be "the Rickiest of the Ricks" (Rick and Morty's Rick C-137), the most truth-oriented version of yourself. That means the least motivated reasoning, the lowest ego and the least self.

chunks.heading: Authenticity: no mask, no false humility
chunks.text:
- Naval defines authenticity as "not putting on a fake persona, not having a mask." We wear masks because we care what others think and want to fit in.
- Inauthenticity includes signaling status, using jargon to sound smart, and claiming to know what you don't or not to know what you do.
- False humility is also an ego trip: "if you're actually low ego, there's no such thing as humility anymore, and there's no such thing as pride."
- When he started tweeting, VCs messaged that he was "not backable" and had gone off the rails. The cost of authenticity is risking embarrassment.
- The payoff is long-term. It removes people around you who only like a persona, ends the walking on eggshells, and gets you out of situations you'd have to force or pretend to stay in.
- He says he is lazy but won't accept bad outcomes: "I have an ability to walk away from suboptimal relationships or situations even if it's painful. I just won't stay in them."
- He dislikes VCs who call themselves "the team behind the team." The founder built the company and took the risk. Few VCs genuinely roll up their sleeves, and they're not the famous ones.

chunks.heading: Explore, then invest: how to choose a career, place and partner
chunks.text:
- Naval says modern life reverses the ancestral setup. In a tribe, rejection and bad choices were costly, reputation was local and people married early. Now it's a search function: you can fly anywhere, enter any career and meet almost any people. That is daunting but means you don't have to stay in a bad situation.
- If you get rejected, "it's like a bad Google search result. Hit back and just search again." You'll meet 10-20,000 people in your life, out of eight billion.
- There are two phases, and you can't skip either:
  - Explore widely until you find the fit.
  - Then invest, because "all the benefits in life come from compound interest."
- What to invest in: a place, people, a business, knowledge, a career, your physical health. Find the work that "feels like play to you and looks like work to others," and a partner who makes you happy by being who they are, as you do for them.
- Failure modes:
  - Too little exploration: people spend 3 weeks job hunting and 5 years in the job.
  - Too much exploration: staying single until 50, then deciding to settle, or never investing in anything. "If you never invest in anything, it's an empty life."
- Weather matters more than you'd think, and he calls it prosaic but real.

chunks.heading: Judgment comes from iterations, not 10,000 hours
chunks.text:
- Naval says Malcolm Gladwell's 10,000 hours is wrong. It is really about iterations, "not repetitions."
- An iteration means: do something, honestly reflect on the outcome, make a change, try again. Do that enough in any endeavor and it develops judgment.
- With judgment you stop trying everything and start rejecting most options, until you know the kind of person, place or work you want. Then you can start investing.
- He notes this is all ex post facto reasoning: easy to see looking back, hard to see moving forward.
- Advice only resonates if the listener has had the experience and now has a word for it. General principles are mental hooks. Specific help needs a back-and-forth (he likes Air Chat and Clubhouse for that), because he can't answer well without knowing someone's situation.
- He says he doesn't want to be only an advice giver. A good life means writing for yourself and your children and doing things that are "useful and beautiful and true." He gives advice only when asked something specific.

chunks.heading: Choose your environment, choose what to want
chunks.text:
- Naval says environment is upstream of your thoughts, and an enlightened mind chooses its own environment. Choosing it consciously is the first step of adapting.
- He holds that you don't owe it to a relationship to struggle through it (unless you have kids), and that you can curate and change relationships.
- His tweet: "The only true test of intelligence is if you get what you want out of life." It is a two-part test: choosing what to want, then getting it. The wants should be achievable, at the edge of your range, and not make the process miserable.
- The first IQ test is whether you stay where you were born. The better place might be the next town or another country.
- If you pass that test, there is little to be envious of. He says no one on earth is someone he'd swap lives with.
- He recommends choosing inspiration over envy. Pull the inspiring part from people, such as Elon and Peter Thiel ("you should do important things, create the definite future you want to live in"), and ignore the rest.
- Steve Jobs gave him license to mix the spiritual and scientific (calligraphy, Zen, LSD, Pixar, NeXT, the fall and return). Jobs embodied his philosophy in products rather than lecturing, which Naval appreciates.
- He thinks Silicon Valley lacks a single cultural leader since Jobs, but there is plenty of mini-inspiration. Pick heroes and traits deliberately.
- Everyone is a "universal explainer" (Deutsch) and capable of anything. We are limited by social scripts. After you figure out the long-term things that make you better off, you can do things that make society better off, because obsessing only on yourself won't make you happy.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Naval revisits his "assets that earn while you sleep" definition of wealth through David Deutsch's lens: wealth is the set of physical transformations you can effect, and knowledge, not capital, is the multiplier. He argues ethical wealth creation is possible and cynicism is self-defeating. He then applies Deutsch to products: good ones are hard to vary, and technology markets carry network effects and scale economies.

chunks.heading: Naval's definition of wealth: assets that earn while you sleep
chunks.text:
- His working definition, shaped by wanting to make money: "assets that earn while you sleep." The goal is to break out of the 9-to-5 trap where input is tied to output.
- He says he always wanted to be "the most successful guy for doing the least work in every aspect of my life." Laziness is a form of leverage: ask for the highest-leverage solution so there is time left for health, children and education.
- Examples of assets that earn while you sleep:
  - Capital: investing means giving up the right to future assets society owed you so businesses can employ people and build things.
  - A piece of a business: a 3D printer, a computer, a GPU cluster training the next AI model, or an organization of people (possibly across time zones) that you check in on.
  - Intellectual property or a piece of media that keeps circulating, and that people pay for or that brings access or notoriety.
- He calls this a good practical definition if the goal is just making money.

chunks.heading: Deutsch's definition: wealth is knowledge, not capital
chunks.text:
- He now prefers David Deutsch's deeper definition: wealth is the set of physical transformations you can effect (bring into existence). It scales from a civilization down to an individual.
- Stored capital is part of it (money buys a backhoe or hires people), but most of the capability comes from technology and leverage. Ten cavemen can't change what ten modern humans can, because of knowledge.
- Knowledge is the big multiplier, not capital. This is one reason he says Marxism fails: value isn't in the factories. "If you removed Elon Musk from SpaceX, you can't capture his wealth. It disappears because the knowledge just disappears." SpaceX is "a group of very intelligent people held together by a common mission," not a pie to divide.
- Gold has little value on its own. It is "a pointer to actual value", which lies in people doing things.
- As a society or individual gains knowledge, they become wealthier. His own earning power is the highest it has been because people know he has knowledge.
- Startups were not what made him popular. Thinking through and articulating ideas was, and that is knowledge too.

chunks.heading: Timeless wisdom vs. transmissible knowledge, and why cliches are fine
chunks.text:
- Technical knowledge (building cars, computers, robots) is transmissible: one person discovers it and others copy it, making everyone wealthier.
- Wisdom (human nature, what a good life is) can't be copied. It must be "recreated inside the listener." You need to hear it a thousand ways in a thousand contexts until it clicks against your own experience.
- Hearing it too early or too many times makes it a cliche. He cites "Row, row, row your boat" as great wisdom packaged to persist, but one that would get laughed at if offered in a book.
- Reply to the "fortune cookie" criticism (Eric's framing: "cliche is Lindy"): he tries to say something true in an interesting way, mostly for himself, and repetition is fine because a new phrasing may stick with someone, or draw a reply that changes his own view.
- Anything not brand new on a timeless topic will be a cliche. The alternative is celebrity or political news, which he finds entertaining but not additive. Truly new technical topics can only be judged by a few qualified people.

chunks.heading: Ethical wealth creation and capitalism
chunks.text:
- Believing ethical wealth creation is possible is a precursor to everything else. Without it, people "get bitter too early" and reject the game.
- Most effort around wealth goes into siphoning, controlling and defending it. He notes that in nature there are about six times as many parasite species as standalone ones. Societies with too many people slicing the pie rather than baking it collapse.
- He argues bank bailouts and cronyism are government intervention (picking winners and losers), not free-market capitalism.
- Capitalism is the minimum viable set of rules so that energy goes into creating property rather than stealing or fighting over it. Its basis is respect for private property: improve land or create something and you keep the improvement. Externalities like pollution and public goods still need handling.
- He wants a "capitalism quality score." He says roughly a third to 40% of US GDP is government-controlled, with another 20-30% under regulation or quasi-government sectors like education and healthcare. The failure case is the best and brightest no longer immigrating.
- Cynicism is self-fulfilling. Despite luck and unfairness, this is the greatest period for wealth creation in history, with more knowledge, capital and leverage than ever. If you are moderately intelligent, hard-working and flexible, you can do extremely well.
- Compounding works, but on 10-30 year timescales: "There's no get-rich quick schemes. That's just someone selling you something."
- Jobs and Musk take on "impossible" tasks because they think: if others can do it, why can't I?

chunks.heading: Truth-seeking systems, skin in the game and accountability
chunks.text:
- Deutsch's method: conjecture, criticism, experiment, then circulate what works. He says it drove progress since the British Enlightenment and is lost by banning criticism (censorship), denying truth, or deferring to "big science."
- He says the textbook scientific method is an idealized fiction. In practice everyone is a little scientist, such as someone testing diets and exercise.
- All truth-seeking systems follow the same loop: conjecture then filter. Science: conjecture and criticism. Business: innovation, then failed companies go out of business. Evolution: mutation, then selection.
- Taleb's skin in the game is isomorphic. It is not just having money at stake; it is that bad risk-takers get weeded out over time (losing capital, life or reputation) and good ones spread the benefits.
- The most ethical thing you can do is be a risk-taker and bear the consequences yourself. Bad capitalism is when others bear your risk.
- He frames accountability as conspicuously, directly and publicly taking the risk with both upside and downside, not risk for its own sake.
- He says Buffett and Munger opposed investment banks going public: partnerships carried personal risk, while a faceless corporation lets executives shift risk to society, get bailed out, and keep their assets.
- Munger's point: people who make unethical behavior impossible (double-entry bookkeeping, the cash register) are effective saints. Ethics is a fuzzy line, and academics and journalists can seem most moral because they build nothing.

chunks.heading: Small groups, competition and the limits of alignment
chunks.text:
- He thinks the biggest impediment to progress is size: of institutions, countries and groups. Large groups seek consensus rather than truth, don't admit mistakes or apologize.
- The best systems are small groups competing, each bearing its own benefits and losses: many religions, city states, and companies. The risk is that competition turns kinetic or consolidates into monopoly.
- The ideal is to federalize: harness competitive energy in virtual, non-violent competition. The US benefited from 50 states running different experiments and from many competing companies. It breaks down with a few big monopolies, banks that capture government, or government running education and healthcare.
- AI alignment: "We can't even align humans. How are we going to align AIs." He says it mostly means the owner putting the AI on a leash.
- Beyond incentive alignment (like giving someone equity) or kinship, aligning strangers comes down to coercion. Every law, even a parking ticket, is ultimately enforced by people with guns, and enforcement becomes preferential as organizations grow.
- He thinks a single global government is the worst outcome, closer to China or Russia, and notes democracies can elect dictators, a one-way street.

chunks.heading: Good products are hard to vary (Deutsch applied to product)
chunks.text:
- A good explanation is hard to vary: change a detail and it breaks, like the one puzzle piece that fits. Good products are the same.
- Example: the iPhone's form factor is still close to its 2007 launch; the laptop form factor hasn't changed either. If you sell multiple versions of a product, "you better have a really good reason."
