- Emergence comes from constraints, not freedom: parts locked together in certain ways produce a new capability. Contracts, marriages and companies are voluntary constraints that make creation possible.
- Good product means removing unnecessary parts (not "Eli 5 simple"). He cites Saint-Exupery's airplane wing: perfect when there's nothing left to take away. Cars converge on one shape because wind-tunnel testing finds the efficient design.
- Technology is "the automation of knowledge": figure something out, automate it, scale it, distribute it. Embedded knowledge is hard to vary. Once batteries are solved, cars go electric: fewer parts, easier repair, cleaner, and a car can recharge itself, which suits self-driving, with swappable batteries enabling 24/7 use.

chunks.heading: Reach, network effects and winner-take-all technology
chunks.text:
- Good products have surprising reach, like good explanations. Jobs' team didn't design the iPhone for oil companies' logistics apps.
- Example: BlackBerry's keyboard was entrenched in enterprise, and Ballmer mocked the iPhone for lacking one. Multi-touch plus a great screen made the keyboard obsolete. Consumers brought iPhones to work, and IT "got outvoted." He expects voice to push keyboards out further.
- Knowledge is what persists and replicates in the environment, like genes. Bad advice that fails doesn't get spread.
- All technology has winner-take-all network effects and scale economies, more obvious in Facebook, WhatsApp and Apple's developer platform, but also Amazon. The internet yields one huge winner plus a long tail and "destroys the mediocre middle", which relied on geography or regulation.
- The best product amortizes development over the largest base and has the most thought-through, bleeding-edge features. Money can't buy a better phone than the latest iPhone or Android, which share a supply chain with hundreds of billions in R&D. Rich people can only buy a weirder one.
- He calls the Tesla Model Y the best all-around car in 2025: a million dollars buys only a goofier car. Trying to buy status is the worst way to signal it.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Naval answers Reddit questions on AI, the gig economy, happiness, habits and early-career startup advice. The business-relevant parts: build an independent brand, go to the startup hub, expect individual ventures to fail but keep taking shots, distrust investor advice because incentives rule, and guard your time fiercely.

chunks.heading: Happiness is a skill and a choice, not an outcome of success
chunks.text:
- Naval says worldly success pulled him away from happiness. He got what he wanted, then noticed peers with similar success "just didn't seem all that happy." He describes strong hedonic adaptation: he got used to anything quickly.
- His conclusion: "happiness is internal," and all real success is internal. External effort still has to be done because humans are biologically wired for it.
- He argues more worldly success builds the ego, increases fear of loss, and deepens concern about what others think.
- He treats happiness as largely the absence of suffering. It comes from peace, which comes from understanding yourself and watching desire, judgment and reaction. He separates it from pleasure, which he sees as momentary.
- Core claim: happiness is "a skill that you develop and a choice that you make." You decide it matters, prioritize it, read everything on it, and work at it like building muscle or learning calculus.
- He thinks Buddhists have done the best work here and modern science has weak answers. He calls the modern world "full of distractions," and says Twitter and Facebook make people unhappy through dispute, comparison, jealousy and anger over things that don't matter.
- Practical hacks he uses:
  - Insight meditation, aimed at understanding how his mind works.
  - Catching himself judging and finding the positive interpretation (once took seconds, now sub-second).
  - More sunlight on skin.
  - Telling friends he is a happy person, so consistency bias keeps him living up to it.
  - Asking "Is it so important to me that I be unhappy unless this goes my way?" when he catches himself desiring something.
  - Dropping caffeine and working out daily ("If you have peace of body, it's easier to have peace of mind").
- He says these hacks won't fix severe depression but can upgrade happiness slightly.
- He quotes a monk, via his brother Kamal: the secret to peace is saying "Yes" to everything that happens. Judging separates you from things and people, leading to loneliness and suffering.

chunks.heading: Not fearing death, and not taking yourself too seriously
chunks.text:
- Naval says an insight he holds that most people don't: "I'm not afraid of death anymore."
- He argues much of life's struggle (building lasting works, businesses, books, even obsession with children) comes from a fear of death and a quest for immortality.
- His reasoning: the universe is vast and old, humans are like "monkeys on a small rock," and our lives are "like a firefly blinking once in the night." Whole civilizations are remembered in a word or two ("Sumerian. Mayan.").
- Whether or not you believe in an afterlife, he says the conclusion is the same: life is short and precious, so "there's no excuse for spending most of your life in misery."
- This is not a license for nihilism or bad behavior. He says to be moral, take care of others, sleep well and enjoy yourself, but "don't take yourself so seriously."
- Stated life philosophy (he says he may change it next year): keep growing and learning, seek truth, accept things as they are, see the world as it really is, and live your life. He thinks deeper goals and ideologies lead to desire, belief systems, disappointment and conflict.
- On planning: he avoids life reviews, quarterly plans and micro-control of himself. He focuses on one or two important things and surrenders the rest, which leaves him able to appreciate everything he already has.

chunks.heading: Habits: the meta-skill of making and breaking them
chunks.text:
- Naval calls learning to break habits "a very important meta-skill that can serve you better in life than almost anything else," and says you only learn it by actually breaking one.
- His cadence: break one bad habit every six months, and pick up one good habit every six months to a year. He says this keeps you from sliding backward and compounds into gradual improvement.
- Daily exercise is his anchor habit. Do the same activity at the same time, seven days a week, early or on waking. It forces other fixes (no late drinking or partying, less caffeine) and teaches how habits work. He says the specific workout matters less than the daily consistency.
- Techniques to break a habit:
  - Substitute something else.
  - Go cold turkey.
  - Wean off gradually.
  - Use social proof by telling others.
  - Stack other habits that leave no time for it.
  - Remove the triggers.
  - Tone down the rewards.
- He lost weight over about a decade through slow habit changes (going paleo, low-carb, cutting processed food), not one epiphany, and says he has almost never slid backward.
- He rereads The Power of Habit to keep in mind that "humans are basically habit machines." Habits give efficiency but also allow addiction and unconscious living.

chunks.heading: What Naval would teach in school and how he approaches learning
chunks.text:
- Curriculum he would run for children: happiness, nutrition, diet, exercise, building and breaking habits, relationships and finding a spouse, meditation, basic skills over memorized facts, and old books that have withstood the test of time.
- Practical add-ons: run a lemonade stand or small business to earn money, do charity work, visit the third world to see real suffering, learn public speaking, business writing, basic persuasion and some programming.
- He would cut chunks of geography, history, second or third languages, and music (unless there is an inclination). Reason: we live in the Wikipedia era, so memorized facts are largely irrelevant; kids will likely not need to drive; and aptitude should guide emphasis.
- On his own education (computers and economics): microeconomics was very useful, macroeconomics mostly useless. Theoretical computer science (math, algorithms) was most useful because it doesn't change, while learning Java or Fortran faded. He'd add more math and physics, plus psychology and evolution, to understand people.
- Principle: "focus on theory and principles over facts." The most important skill is knowing how to learn; with good math and a love of reading, "there's nothing you can't learn on your own."
- Reading habit: he keeps around 50 books on Kindle plus several physical books, reads by mood and by chapter rather than sequentially, and finds this makes him read regularly. He says rereading the greats beats reading something not as great.
- Books he named:
  - Matt Ridley (Genome, The Red Queen, Origins of Virtue, The Rational Optimist, The Evolution of Everything).
  - The Lessons of History (Durant).
  - The Prophet (Gibran).
  - Perfectly Reasonable Deviations (Feynman).
  - The Power of Myth (Campbell).
  - Mastering the Core Teachings of the Buddha (Daniel Ingram).
  - Total Freedom (Krishnamurti).
  - Bed of Procrustes (Taleb).
  - Science fiction such as Greg Egan.

chunks.heading: Working in a post-corporate economy and building an independent brand
chunks.text:
- Naval applies Coase's 1937 paper: the industrial revolution pulled people into hierarchies because factories required scale. Information technology now lowers communication and transaction costs, so people can work through computers as independent contractors.
- Examples he cites: Uber driving (a weaker example), freelancers finding work through Twitter and online sources, and AngelList startup jobs. Marketplaces he names include Pick Crew, Gigster, Elance, Craigslist and oDesk.
- Example of the better version: a world-class journalist no longer needs the New York Times. Start a blog or Twitter in spare time, build an independent brand, and late in the curve (YouTube star or popular blogger) charge for access and earn from books and newsletters, working from anywhere.
- His advice for the next 20 years:
  - Find something you love and have a shot at being among the best in the world at it.
  - Build an independent brand around your own name, not a company's.
  - Do creative work, because anything not creative can be replicated by society and then underpaid.
  - Get comfortable with boom-bust work (a few weeks busy, a few weeks off).
- Timing: "It will be gradual, and then it will be sudden." The best preparation is to not give up your independence in the first place.

chunks.heading: Startup careers, locations and long-run effort
chunks.text:
- To enter startups without money or connections, Naval's answer is to move to San Francisco or another startup hub: Austin, LA, New York, Boston, Berlin, London, Bangalore, Shanghai, or parts of Delhi or Beijing. "All the other people who are in startups are in these places, so you have to get in the flow." The same logic applies to any industry: actors go to Hollywood, finance people go to New York, London or Hong Kong.
- Ways in once there: learn to code at App Academy, Hack Reactor or General Assembly; volunteer for startups; start in customer service or operations. He says startups are moved forward by people willing to do the work, and with that attitude "you'll figure your way out within a couple of years."
- On choosing between big tech, early-stage startups, bootstrapping or a VC-funded company: it is "highly, highly contextual."
  - If you know the company, the cofounders and the space, go do it.
  - If not, get as close to it as possible by joining a very early startup.
  - If you want lifestyle and steady money for family, join a later-stage startup clearly on the path to success.
  - Startups are a young person's game. He suggests taking at least one shot before 30 or 35, though older founders exist.
- Treat advice from investors as self-serving. "Incentives are everything... Incentives are superpowers."
- Long-run view, paraphrasing Charlie Munger: get up early, work hard, learn something every day, and if you live long enough you eventually get what you deserve. Investing taught him how much randomness there is. He notes "individual entrepreneurial efforts often fail, but individual entrepreneurs over their careers rarely fail" as long as they keep taking shots and getting back up.
- He made a small fortune in the 1999 dot-com bubble and lost it by holding too long. He says that was a good lesson, because later money was respected as rare and hard to make. He says people who win early often learn the wrong lessons.
- For people on US visas wanting to start a company while keeping a job, he points to Unshackled (unshackled.co), an accelerator he has a small investment in.

chunks.heading: Guarding time, saying no, and choosing who you work with
chunks.text:
- Naval calls inbound requests for coffees, meetings and calls "the bane of my existence." He once owned idontdocoffee.com and replied from it, but now calls that rude and petulant. He has since become skilled at avoiding time-sucking meetings.
- Core claim: "Time is all you have in this world." Being busy kills productivity and happiness. As you age you have more obligations, so you must be ruthless.
- Heuristic he endorses from Derek Sivers: it's "Hell yes" or "No." If he's not excited, he doesn't do it.
- Keep empty space on the calendar. He recommends at least one day a week, preferably budgeting two, with no meetings, just thinking time. "It's only after you're bored that you have the great ideas." Also leave room for serendipity from new people.
- He says people generally don't disrespect you for declining; they often want your time more because you are discriminating with it.
- His most popular tweet: "If you can't see yourself working with somebody for life, don't work with them for a day." He doesn't say to refuse people literally; he says to treat early time as a search function across jobs, partners and hobbies, then go all-in on the people and things you love, because "all the greatness in life comes from compound interest, whether it's in investments or it's in relationships."
- Five chimps theory: a chimp's mood and behavior can be predicted by the five chimps it spends the most time with, so "choose your five chimps carefully," ideally happy people.
- On conflict: he admits he handles it poorly and gets angry, so he tries to notice the anger and its bodily signs before reacting. His best advice is not to associate with high-conflict people, because someone always fighting others will eventually fight you. He drifts away from them without announcing it.
- Money has a steep discount rate with age. His test: how many years of youth would you trade for losing all your money and job while keeping friends and family? For him it's about two to three years, and he says the number shrinks as you get older.

chunks.heading: Artificial intelligence: general vs specific
chunks.text:
- Naval doubts general-purpose AI is close. He says people who talk about Skynet-style AI don't write much code, since no fundamental breakthroughs have been made; current work is similar code run faster or on more data. The brain works very differently from computers.
- On the Turing test: he thinks we are "barely any closer" than 20 or 30 years ago.
- Possible exception: an emergent "social AI" arising from all the world's computers networked together. He expects it to emerge slowly and softly, not self-modify like a classic general AI, and to be built to serve humans and woven into the human fabric.
- Investing view: he is not worried about general-purpose AI and does not think general-purpose AI companies have much of a future. Specific AI companies solving narrow problems (computer vision, self-driving cars, self-piloting drones) "could be very real," using lots of data, processing power and good code.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Naval explains how founders of hot late-stage companies can raise money without surrendering control, why raising less keeps companies faster, and how to vet investors. He also covers hiring discipline, early founder liquidity, and giving early employees founder-level equity.

chunks.heading: Control matters more than valuation in late-stage rounds
chunks.text:
Naval's rule from Venture Hacks: "Valuation is temporary. Control is forever." Whoever holds control can later dictate your valuation too, so he says never give it up.

- Control leaks out through protective provisions. They were meant to shield preferred holders as minority shareholders, but they hand over real control.
- A veto on future fundraising gives that investor a lock on the company. If you need money, they have to agree, "which means they run the place."
- The same applies to vetoes on option pool expansion and new share issuances to employees.
- M&A is "the big one, where the biggest fights happen". Preferred holders can push for the opposite outcome from what founders want.
- Late-stage rounds are increasingly done by mutual funds, strategics and family offices, not only VCs. Naval says this lets a hot company build a custom bundle and keep control.

chunks.heading: Selling common stock and the fallback ladder of concessions
chunks.text:
For a hot, high-growth company with multiple bidders, Naval would sell common stock ("the ultimate hack"). That means no board seats and no vetoes on M&A, option pool issuance or future fundraising. He notes this only works when there are multiple bidders. If the investor won't take that, he steps down through these options:

1. Common plus a liquidation preference. "That's it. I would be leaving out all the other junk."
2. Protective provisions only for non-arm's-length transactions, such as self-dealing, stock issued to a friend, or selling the company to a brother. Arm's-length, bona fide deals need no approval. He says investors should always keep a veto on insider self-dealing.
3. A veto that belongs to the preferred class as a whole, not each series. If the other investors go along, the later-stage investors must too. Earlier investors are usually people you chose carefully and trust more.
4. Founder shares with extra voting power. This works only up to a point.

Some rights cannot be contracted away under Delaware and California law. His examples: under California law (as of 2003), each series must separately approve an M&A. And in Delaware, even a small shareholder can demand your financials through inspection rights.

chunks.heading: Why liquidation preference fades after the early stages
chunks.text:
Naval explains the original purpose with an example.

- A company raises at a $9M pre-money valuation. An investor puts in $1M, so post-money is $10M and the investor owns 10%.
- If the company then just divvied up that $1M among shareholders, the founder would get $900,000 and the investor $100,000.
- The preference exists to prevent that. It protects the investor on a distribution of cash, not against a general downside.

As preferences stack on in later rounds, they become "a giant freebie." Naval's evidence is that public markets are all common stock. If a company is really worth $900M and someone invests $100M, nobody will shut it down and hand back the $100M, because that would throw away $900M of real value.

- "You'd be a fool to do a seed round buying common stock." The preference is "really, really important at the early stages."
- It makes no sense at later stages and is gone at the public stage.

chunks.heading: Secondaries and founder liquidity
chunks.text:
Naval says secondaries are becoming more common, and "secondary markets are here to stay."

- Founder and investor incentives diverge more over time. Funds keep getting larger, so a $100M exit can make a founder happy while disappointing the investors.
- Odds of success have fallen. He guesses a venture-backed company's odds were about 1 in 10 in 1999 and might be 1 in 50 now. There are many more companies, the markets are winner-take-all, and the half-life of winners is shorter.
- He quotes a friend who called incubator graduates "the locust swarm of startups," so every business is under constant assault.
- Founders get "a couple of shots on goal" in life. Good VCs who ask for a billion-dollar outcome must let founders take some off the table along the way.

When to ask:

- Never take substantial liquidity if the investors end up losing all their money.
- Start asking once you are convinced, "almost beyond a shadow of a doubt," that the company's value exceeds the stack of liquidation preferences. Evidence is enough revenue or cash flow, or acquisition offers above the preference stack.
- The conversation usually starts with an acquisition offer that investors want you to refuse. A smart investor will then let you take something off the table.
- Secondaries are rare at seed, A and B. They are common from C onward, and sometimes at B if the company has made substantial progress.

chunks.heading: Companies need less money than they think, and raising more makes you slower
chunks.text:
Naval calls this "the single most important elephant in the room." Companies don't need as much money as they used to, though he says hardware and local expansion are exceptions.

- Software is open source, hardware sits on AWS, marketing runs on Google, Twitter, Facebook, the App Store and similar channels, and many engineers are outsourced.
- His examples of small teams with huge value: Satoshi Nakamoto, WhatsApp (about 50 people, bought for $19B), YouTube (probably under 60 people when bought), and Instagram (a few people).
- He cites Slack, which said it had 50 or 100 years of money and was still raising. He guesses much of that went to secondary or acquisitions and calls those "not the classic reasons."
- Enterprise companies are heading the same way. Slack barely has a sales force. Bigger companies like Slack and Uber still need fewer resources than the version of them five or ten years earlier.

Why founders raise anyway: money is cheap, and it works as insurance, a scorecard, an acquisition tool, and a way to pay for hiring.

The costs:

- "When you raise more money you do spend more money," however disciplined you are.
- You move slower, meetings grow, and more stakeholders must be coordinated.
- You lose focus and take on too many projects. Cash-constrained companies tend to do better.
- Example: Pierre Omidyar's eBay. He credited his success to being the only competitor without much outside financing for a long time. Rivals put people into every transaction. With no headcount, he built an automated rating system and scalable processes from day one, and ran away with the market.

chunks.heading: Choosing investors and new capital sources
chunks.text:
Naval thinks family offices, hedge funds, PE and foreign funds are good for entrepreneurs.

- Venture capital is "a bundle of advice, control, and money." More capital sources let you unbundle it: advice from people you want, money from the cheapest source, and leave the control behind.
- VCs calling these players "dumb money" is like a laundromat owner angry that another one opened. "Always filter venture advice through venture incentives."
- Downsides: they can be hot money and may not do their pro-rata. They may also try to veto things they shouldn't, and corporate contacts can get swapped out. Fix this by not giving them control and not counting on more money from them later.
- Control who sits on your board, or who the relationship person is, if you give a seat.
- "You cannot take someone's money without having a moral, ethical obligation to them." Avoid getting sued by investors, because that makes you untouchable later.

How to vet them:

- "People's true motivations and behavior are revealed, not said." Someone who spends ten minutes telling you how honest they are is dishonest.
- Reference-check hard and spend time with them.
- Watch how they behave in the term sheet process: quick, easy and sensible is a good sign. An exploding term sheet or inflexibility means "ten times worse once the money is in."
- Don't be afraid to call off the close. "I've done it and I've never regretted it." You are effectively "married" to investors, and the dating period is a week to a year.
- Ask an early-stage investor or trusted friend with a good nose who says unpopular things. Be careful of investors chasing a brand-name markup.

chunks.heading: Hiring slowly and rethinking equity
chunks.text:
On headcount:

- Hire extremely slowly, "only after there's a burning need." People tire and hire someone to do their job, and it takes two hires to replace them. That is how a simple web app ends up with thousands of staff.
- Be ruthless about firing and trimming. Founders must watch waste closely, and "there's always waste." He says this has worked for him.

On equity:

- Stock is better than no stock but outdated. AngelList uses six-year vests, and VC firms use ten-year vests.
- As a company matures, grants should shift toward profit sharing, revenue sharing or bonuses. RSUs are diffuse in a large company, since one person can't move performance much.
- A hack: give small standard grants at first, then either substantially raise a person's grant next year or let them go.
- Profit sharing can be tax inefficient. AngelList is an LLC with one layer of taxation, which suits it.

Early employees:

- Naval says it is the lowest-risk time ever to be a founder, yet early employees take founder-level risk without founder-level equity.
- The old split was a founder at 40% and the first employee at 0.15% to 0.25%. He says those days are ending.
- Early employees before product/market fit are "really just hiring late founders." He suggests 1-4% instead of 0.1-0.4%.
- The problem isn't a shortage of engineers but "a surplus of founders," so early engineers have a high opportunity cost.

Who wins in the Valley, risk-adjusted, besides VCs: people who join companies just after product/market fit and help scale them, such as the next Dropbox or Airbnb.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Naval reflects that his early companies were driven by wanting to be a founder, then by money and power, and neither was a great motivation. His best outcomes came from following genuine curiosity. Now he builds only what he wants to exist, with people he admires, because creating beats consuming.

chunks.heading: Naval's early motivations for starting companies were impure
chunks.text:
- Naval says his first few companies were driven by wanting to be a founder: "I really just wanted to be a founder." That desire "kind of overrode everything" and "was not a pure motivation."
- His motivation then shifted to money and power. He says "nobody wants to talk about it, but [money and power] are fundamental drivers."
- He admits wanting both to make money and to have a company with influence, and says "that wasn't that great of a motivation either."
- He wishes he had the insight he has now "20-30 years ago."

chunks.heading: Genuine curiosity produced his best outcomes
chunks.text:
- Looking back, Naval says he was most successful when he took on projects "because I was genuinely curious about them."
- Following his own intellectual curiosity gave him insight, and that insight led to good investments, startups, and outcomes.
- The implication he draws is that curiosity-led work beat founder-identity, money, or status as a starting point.

chunks.heading: The two questions Naval asks before building something
chunks.text:
- Now that he doesn't need to work for money or status, he only works on products he wants to see exist.
- He asks himself: "What's a beautiful thing I can make that wouldn't exist if I didn't put effort into it?"
- He pairs it with a second question: "And what people do I want to spend all my time around?"
- Together these select for both the thing being built and the team building it.

chunks.heading: Why meeting material desires doesn't end the search for purpose
chunks.text:
- Naval argues that once your material desires are somewhat met, "you end up extremely bored."
- When you no longer have to hustle for a living, you can lose your sense of purpose: "What do I do?"
- He rejects two escape routes:
  - Meditating in a corner for a long time "gets boring too."
  - Going completely hedonistic is "a death trap and just an empty lifestyle."

chunks.heading: Creating as self-actualization, done with friends
chunks.text:
- Naval's answer is self-actualization: "I want to be the best version of myself." For him that means creating something.
- He holds that "it's better to create than to consume."
- He finds it "far more fulfilling to learn along the way and build."
- He wants to build with friends, "people that I really respect, admire, and enjoy spending time with."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Naval explains how he approaches decisions (leverage, mental models, systems over goals), why compounding only works with long-term people, and what he looks for in founders and counterparties. Much of the interview covers reading, happiness and education, which is not business-relevant. The business and decision-making material is the durable part.

chunks.heading: Naval on decision-making as leverage and avoiding mistakes
chunks.text:
- Naval argues "decision-making is everything." Someone right 80% of the time instead of 70% gets valued and paid hundreds of times more, because of leverage.
- Example: managing $1 billion and being right 10% more often than someone else is worth $100 million on a judgment call. Technology, large workforces and capital leverage decisions more every year.
- He sees the brain as a memory prediction machine. "X happened in the past, therefore X will happen in the future" is a poor method. He wants principles and mental models instead.
- His best mental model sources are evolution, game theory, Charlie Munger, Nassim Taleb and Benjamin Franklin. Complexity theory taught him the limits of prediction, so he works in the face of ignorance.
- He does not try to say what will work. He eliminates what will not. "Being successful is just about not making mistakes."
- He rejects checklists for investors and entrepreneurs. He thinks Gawande's *Checklist Manifesto* suits pilots and surgeons, not founders.
- He asks three questions: can he trust this person, what are the real odds this works, and how much margin of safety he has if it does.

chunks.heading: Naval's portfolio system: see many, bet small, double down on winners
chunks.text:
- Naval says he does not believe in specific goals. He quotes Scott Adams: "Set up systems, not goals."
- His approach is to find environments where he can thrive and build a system so success is statistically likely. He wants to be successful in 999 of 1,000 universes, not to be the most successful person.
- His investing system: look at 10,000 companies, pick 500 that have a shot at being huge, and keep the option to double down on the 5 winners.
- He does not think he can look at 100 companies, pick 10 winners and go all in. He says he lacks that ability.
- He likes angel and venture bets for their asymmetry. The downside is 1x, and the upside can be 10,000x. "I've tried to rig the game."
- He calls origin stories about success ex-post-facto reasoning. He judges skill by who is consistently successful, since Silicon Valley has many one-hit wonders.
- By his own account, he is no longer in it for the money. He wants to create something new that the world values, that fits his morals, and that he would buy himself.
- Money has steep diminishing returns for him. He calls it "a boat anchor around my neck": something to fear losing, argue about, and have others ask for.

chunks.heading: What Naval looks for in founders and business partners
chunks.text:
- The best founders are long-term thinkers. They are laying "bricks in the foundation of the skyscraper," not building a house, so they fix small things early.
- He wants someone who knows the space well, understands how hard it is, does not care, and commits for the long haul.
- He cites Steve Case: "vision without execution is a hallucination." Passion and vision are not enough. The founder also needs execution and domain depth, deep enough to be contrarian.
- Ideas are not new. All ideas have been thought of, so the value is in idea plus execution plus passion.
- His Steve Jobs example: Jobs did not invent the smartphone idea. He had a very high design bar, understood manufacturing tolerances, rallied people and resources, and took $1 salary at Apple.
- Luck matters in tech: timing, market forces, regulation, platform shifts and open source. He says you cannot predict outsized successes, but you can predict failures, such as a founder who is out of their depth or a short-term thinker.
- Short-term thinkers should find something they can commit to for 10 years. He says that is the minimum time to a good outcome.
- Great people tend to have great outcomes in Silicon Valley, but only on a long timescale. Everyone he judged very capable 20 years ago "almost without exception" became extremely successful.

chunks.heading: How Naval tests integrity and trust in deals
chunks.text:
- He uses Buffett's criteria of intelligence, energy and integrity, and says integrity is the hardest to judge.
- Long-term signal: you have known the person a while. Short-term signal: watch how they treat other people.
- Red flag: someone who is self-dealing toward a partner while saying "I'm taking advantage of that person because they deserve it. You're my friend and I would never do that to you."
- Red flag: someone who talks a lot about how honest they are. He also cites *The Art of Manipulation*, which says con men push the deal too hard and talk up their honesty.
- High-integrity people have an internal moral compass and will not make unfair deals, because it would soil their view of themselves. They are easy to negotiate with and give things they do not need to.
- He argues unhappy deals get unwound and become short-term relationships with no compounding benefit.
- His rule when someone he respects behaves badly: warn them once, then distance himself because "nobody changes." His saying: "the closer you want to get to me, the better your values have to be."
- He adds Buffett's rule, "praise specifically, criticize generally," so egos work for you, not against you.

chunks.heading: Naval's foundational values for business and relationships
chunks.text:
- He defines values as things he will not compromise on.
- Honesty: he never wants to be somewhere he has to watch what he says. Disconnecting thoughts from words creates "multiple threads" in the mind.
- Long-term thinking: he refuses short-term thinking or dealing, and will stop doing business with someone who deals short-term with others. "All the benefits in life come from compound interest" (money, relationships, health, habits).
- He works only with people he expects to stay around for life, and only on things with long-term payoff.
- Peer relationships only: no one above him, none below.
- No anger, and no anger around him.
- He argues ethics is "long-term selfish" but costs in the short term: "If being ethical were profitable, everybody would do it."
- He quotes his trainer: "Easy choices, hard life. Hard choices, easy life." It applies to values, saving for a rainy day and relationships.
- When values line up, small things stop mattering. Quarrels usually mean values do not align.

chunks.heading: Naval on time, commitments and priorities
chunks.text:
- His "two-factor authentication on your calendar" idea: present-him is tired and hungry, while future-him is imagined as high-energy, and present-him keeps promising on future-him's behalf.
- Fix: write a commitment down and check in 48 hours later with a clear mind. Better: commit only to what he would do right now, which matches Derek Sivers' "hell yes or no."
- He says he is in the exploitation phase, not exploration, and still finds it hard to say no.
- "I don't have time" means "it's not a priority." A fuzzy basket of 10 or 15 priorities gets none done.
- He made his own health first (physical, then mental, then spiritual, then family), so the daily morning workout always happens. It was "a complete game-changer."
- He avoids rigid schedules and wants to drop 40, 60 or 80 hour weeks, 9-to-5s and fixed roles. He asks only whether he is doing what he wants, productive and happy.
- He reads 1 to 2 hours a day and says that alone accounts for any material success and intelligence he has.

chunks.heading: Naval on specific knowledge, reality and where returns come from
chunks.text:
- Each person has specific knowledge, capability and desire that no one else has, from the "combinatorics of human DNA and development." Do not copy others' checklists or frameworks.
- "Your goal in life is to find out the people who need you the most, … the business that needs you the most, … the project and the art that needs you the most."
- Returns come from leaving the herd. Best sellers serve social approval. He recommends original sources: Adam Smith, Darwin, Franklin, Munger.
- The smartest and most successful people he knows started out as outcasts, which pushed them to find their own path.
- Real understanding is first principles. "If you can't explain it to a child, then you don't know it." Complicated language is "the mark of a charlatan." Memorizing without being able to rederive from basics is useless.
- To see reality, get the ego out of the way. The stronger the desire for an outcome, the less likely you see the truth.
- Business failure is often a delayed reality check. To avoid self-delusion, he admits problems publicly to co-founders and coworkers.
- He gave up macroeconomics as "junk science" but calls microeconomics and game theory fundamental to business: supply and demand, labor versus capital, tit for tat.
- He prefers micro over macro generally: change yourself, then family and neighbors, before changing the world.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Naval walks through his "How to Get Rich" tweetstorm. Wealth is owned assets that earn while you sleep, built with specific knowledge, accountability, leverage and judgment, not rented time. Code and media are permissionless leverage, and long-term games with ethical, high-integrity partners compound. Also covers business models (network effects, scale economies, price discrimination) and hourly-rate discipline.

chunks.heading: Wealth, money and status are three different things
chunks.text:
- Naval defines wealth as "assets that earn while you sleep": businesses, code running at night, money reinvested into other assets. A house counts only if it can be rented out.
- Wealth buys freedom, meaning no tie, no 7 a.m. commute, no boss. He says Ferraris, yachts and jets "get really boring and stupid, really fast."
- Money is how wealth is transferred. He calls it social IOUs for value you created in the past, which governments debase by printing more.
- Status is rank in a social hierarchy and is zero-sum. Wealth is positive-sum: one person having a house does not stop another from having one.
- People who attack wealth creators are usually playing the status game. Journalists attacking rich people or the tech industry are "bidding for status." He advises avoiding status games because they make you angry and combative.
- Society can only carry a small share of takers: "If you get too many takers, and not enough makers, society falls apart." His example is Venezuela.
- He means ethical wealth: voluntary exchange, not monopolies, crony capitalism or mispriced externalities.

chunks.heading: Making money is not luck: the four kinds of luck
chunks.text:
- Naval wants to be wealthy in 999 of 1,000 parallel universes, not in the 50 where he got lucky. He claims that if dropped on a street in any English-speaking country, he would be wealthy again in 5 to 10 years.
- Four kinds of luck (from Marc Andreessen's post):
  1. Blind luck, which is fate.
  2. Luck from hustle, where lots of motion stirs things up.
  3. Luck from preparation, where skill lets you spot breaks others miss.
  4. Luck from your unique character and reputation, where opportunity finds you. Example: the best deep-sea diver gets paid when someone finds a sunken treasure ship.
- Type 4 is the one to aim for. Trusted, high-integrity deal makers get approached by people who need deals done safely (his example is Warren Buffett).
- Quotes he and Nivi cite: "extreme people get extreme results" (Sam Altman) and "you can't be normal and expect abnormal returns" (Jeffrey Pfeffer).
- His own wealth came in "chips," not one payout. His first fortune was lost in the stock market, and in his second he was cheated by business partners. The third attempt worked, built from many small businesses and investments.
- Networking and coffee meetings mostly rely on Type 1 and Type 2 luck. He says a busy calendar and a busy mind "will destroy your ability to do great things."

chunks.heading: Equity, not hours: why you can't rent out your time
chunks.text:
- "You are not going to get rich renting out your time. You must own equity, a piece of the business."
- Salaried work ties inputs to outputs. You do not earn while asleep, and employers pay "the bare minimum" to get the job done. Even rich doctors get there through a private practice, brand or IP.
- Look for work where inputs and outputs are disconnected. One engineer can create Bitcoin, while another ships a year of unused code. A lumberjack is at best about 3x better than the worst lumberjack.
- Tools and creativity create that disconnect. Replaceable, teachable roles will eventually be automated.
- Live below your means. "The most dangerous things are heroin and a monthly salary" (he attributes this to Taleb, unsure). Lifestyle upgrades reset what you think wealth is.
- Ideally money arrives in "discrete lumps" years apart, as in tech: a decade of losses, then a payday in year 11. He argues high marginal tax rates punish that pattern.

chunks.heading: Give society what it wants but can't yet get, at scale
chunks.text:
- Naval says you get rich by giving society "what it wants, but does not yet know how to get, at scale."
- Technology is whatever doesn't work yet (he credits Danny Hillis, after an in-text correction). Rockefeller's oil, Ford's cars and Jobs's smartphone were once technology.
- Step 1: find something natural to you and within your skills that society will want. Step 2: figure out how to scale it so everyone can have one.
- Nivi's framing, which Naval extends: the entrepreneur brings the high end to the mass market. Rich people had chauffeurs, then Uber, then scooters.
- The internet connects everyone to everyone, so any niche obsession can find 50,000 passionate people. His examples: Joe Rogan reportedly near $100M a year, PewDiePie's reach, e-sports, and miniature-cooking channels.
- "Escape competition through authenticity." Nobody can compete with you on being you, so don't copy.
- Pick a business model with leverage:
  - **Scale economies:** widget 10,000 is cheaper than widget 5.
  - **Zero marginal cost of reproduction:** Rogan's podcast number 1,100 pays far more than number 1, with no extra effort.
  - **Network effects:** Metcalfe's law says value grows with the square of nodes (10 nodes = 100, 100 nodes = 10,000). The number one player wins everything unless you are number two. Examples: Facebook, Uber vs Lyft, Google, Twitter, YouTube, Amazon Prime.
- Network effect defined: each additional user adds value to existing users. Design hooks so customers add value to each other: "You're sleeping at night and your customers are adding value to each other."
- Cautionary tale: Epinions drifted into the comparison-shopping fight with DealTime, mySimon, PriceGrabber, NexTag and Bizrate. Amazon won e-tail and that space "went to zero." He says they should have pushed into local reviews, which became Yelp and TripAdvisor, because a review of a scarce item like a restaurant is worth more than the 1,000th camera review. Lesson: "play stupid games, win stupid prizes."

chunks.heading: The four types of leverage, and why code and media win
chunks.text:
- Archimedes' line, "Give me a lever long enough," frames the point: fortunes require leverage.
- **Labor** is the oldest and most overvalued. People ask "how many people work there?" He calls it "the worst form of leverage": messy, requires leadership, and a short hop from mutiny. Use the minimum labor needed to access the other types.
- **Capital** dominated the last century (bankers, Buffett types). It is surgical and scales well, but you first need specific knowledge and accountability to be given any.
- **Code and media** (products with no marginal cost of replication) are where the new fortunes are made: Rogan, PewDiePie, Bezos, Zuckerberg, Page, Gates, Jobs.
- Code and media are permissionless. Nobody has to follow you or fund you. Coding, writing, podcasting and YouTube need no one's approval.
- "The robot army is already here": servers running code while you sleep. Coding is the superpower for commanding them, and the bottleneck is deciding what to tell them to do.
- Tech startups combine all three: minimum high-output labor (engineers, designers), capital for marketing and scale, and code/media.
- Code and media products are egalitarian. Bezos has no better search or Netflix than you. Labor- and capital-based goods are not; status goods like a Rolex only work if few have them.
- The best products target the middle class, where scale amortizes cost. A Toyota Corolla or a Tesla Model 3 beats a Lamborghini for daily use.
- Wealth built on code and media is more ethical because the output reaches everyone.

chunks.heading: Specific knowledge, accountability and judgment
chunks.text:
- To get paid at scale: accountability is why you, leverage is the scale, and specific knowledge is why you rather than someone else.
- **Specific knowledge cannot be trained.** If a class could teach it, others could be trained, then software, then robots. It is found by following genuine curiosity and natural aptitude, "the thing that feels like play to you but looks like work to others." It usually sits on the frontier of technology, art or communication.
- Naval's mother told him at 15 or 16 that he would go into business, after watching him critique local pizza parlors. He had planned to be an astrophysicist.
- It is often learned through apprenticeship. Buffett offered to work for Benjamin Graham for free; Graham said "you're overpriced." A cheap apprenticeship in a skill nobody can teach yet is worth it.
- Don't assemble skills too deliberately. Follow obsession and keep an eye on commercial aspects. The Scott Adams skill stack idea (top 25% at several things) works because combinations make you scarce.
- Two forms:
  - **Timely:** machine learning, which may become second hat.
  - **Timeless:** persuasion, which you pick up early and is always valuable.
- Learn to sell and learn to build; "if you can do both, you will be unstoppable" (Musk, Jobs). Bill Gates: "I'd rather teach an engineer marketing than a marketer engineering."
- If forced to pick one: start by building, since it cuts through the noise, then transition to selling because sales skill and reputation scale better and building burns you out.
- **Accountability** means putting your name on things. "Accountability is reputational skin in the game," and people need to be able to tell what role you played. It is like taking equity in your own work: you are paid last but get unlimited upside.
- Fear of public failure holds people back. People who can fail in public gain power. Ruin in business now comes mostly from integrity failures (Madoff), not economic failure.
- A well-functioning team is small with clear owners for product, messaging, fundraising and pricing.
- **Judgment** is knowing the long-term consequences of your actions. In an age of near-infinite leverage it is the decisive skill: a CEO who is 10 to 20% better steering a $100B company is worth hundreds of millions.
- Judgment needs experience. Intellect without skin in the game is "often worse than useless," and the best-judgment people are the least emotional. "The more outraged someone is, the worse their judgment."
- Buffett's credibility (accountable, right in public, high integrity) means "nobody asks him how hard he works."
- Top investors read philosophy and history, not investment books, because investing is real-world and constantly competed away.

chunks.heading: Choosing partners, markets and how you work
chunks.text:
- **Play long-term games with long-term people.** All returns come from compounding in iterated games (tit-for-tat in an iterated prisoner's dilemma). Switching industries resets your network and trust to zero.
- Pick partners with high intelligence, high energy and high integrity, with no compromise on any. "A smart and hard-working crook" is the failure case of skipping integrity.
- Judge integrity by actions: how someone treats a waiter, how they treat enemies. People who loudly advertise their integrity are suspect, like con men.
- His example: a founder kept putting personal money into a failing company through three pivots without wiping out investors, and said "I didn't do it for you... it's my own self-esteem." Naval's gloss: "self-esteem is the reputation that you have with yourself."
- You can't sell someone into lasting motivation; it has to be intrinsic. He won't hire or start a company with someone who isn't into the task.
- Partner with rational optimists. Cynics and pessimists are self-fulfilling and want a fourth option beyond lead, follow or get out of the way. Successful people have an action bias. We descend from pessimists who survived tigers, but modern downside is limited and upside unlimited.
- Avoid ruin: stay out of jail and avoid total capital loss ("it's never worth it to wear an orange jumpsuit"). The Kelly criterion idea: don't bet everything on one gamble, since averages across 100 people are not what one person playing 100 times gets (his Russian roulette example).
- Ethics is "long-term greedy." Honesty frees mental energy and filters out people who want pretty lies. Fair dealers become market hubs that people route deals through; unethical deals pay off only in the short run.
- Work as hard as you can, but what you work on and who you work with come first. Think "product-market-founder fit," three legs of a stool. Pick the startup with the best alumni network (the PayPal mafia).
- Nobody really works 80 to 120 high-output hours. Work in sprints "like a lion hunting," with rest. "Inspiration is perishable," so act when it hits. "Impatience with actions, patience with results."
- Be too busy to "do coffee" yet keep an uncluttered calendar. Decline meetings ruthlessly: push to a call, then email, then text. He says "I don't do non-transactional meetings." Busy people meet you if you show proof of work, like product progress, "an unfake-able resume."
- Reject most advice. Founders who get rich quickly are "giving you their winning lottery ticket numbers." The best founders listen to everyone, then make up their own minds. Avoid anyone who makes money selling how-to-get-rich courses, since "there are no get rich quick schemes."

chunks.heading: Hourly rate, learning and microeconomic concepts
chunks.text:
- Set an aspirational hourly rate that feels absurdly high; his was $5,000/hour before he had money. Outsource or skip anything that costs less than your rate (errands, returns, cooking), and don't penny-pinch if wealth is your top priority.
- Paul Graham's advice for startups: work on product, exercise and eat well, and not much else.
- Learning:
  - "Read what you love until you love to read."
  - Start with foundational, original works (Wealth of Nations, Origin of Species, Feynman's Six Easy Pieces).
  - Mathematics and logic come first. Better to read a great book slowly than fly through a hundred.
  - He names reading, writing, arithmetic, persuasion and programming as the five core skills.
- "There is no skill called business." Skip business school case studies and magazines. Study microeconomics, game theory, psychology, persuasion, ethics, math and computers. Skip macroeconomics ("a branch of politics").
- "Doing is faster than watching." Learning scales with the number of iterations, not hours. Run lots of small experiments, and tolerate frequent small failures. Entrepreneurs "bleed every day" for a big win later.
- Pricing and economics concepts he uses:
  - **Price discrimination:** charge by propensity to pay with a real extra. Business class costs 5 to 10x for perhaps 2 to 3x the airline's cost. Enterprise software does it with freemium tiers charging 10 to 100x for security and admin features.
  - **Consumer surplus:** he'd pay $20 for his Starbucks coffee. All businesses generate it, and Amazon likely generates trillions of dollars of it.
  - **Net present value:** a startup grant of 0.1% of a "$1B" company is worth $10,000, not $1M, if the last round priced it at a $10M valuation.
  - **Negotiation:** "won by whoever cares less." Turn short-term games into repeat games with references, follow-on projects and reviews.
  - **Principal-agent problem:** "If you want it done, Go. If not, Send." Be generous with lieutenants on ownership, prefer boutique firms (a lawyer or banker of one) for accountability, and as an employee think like the owner.
  - **Mispriced externalities:** price them high (water, pollution) instead of using feel-good bans.

chunks.heading: Building a career: ownership, size, and the end goal
chunks.text:
- Real estate ladder showing more specific knowledge, accountability and leverage at each rung: day laborer ($15 to $75/hour, no leverage), general contractor (takes risk and equity), property developer (capital leverage), famous architect or large developer, REIT, then a real estate tech company (the Zillow/Redfin/Trulia type) with all leverage types combined.
- "Productize yourself": scale something authentic to you with leverage. Find hobbies that make you money, keep you fit, and make you smarter. His are reading and making money.
- Ceteris paribus, you will do better in a smaller organization (more accountability, battlefield promotions). Move from large companies to progressively smaller ones; the reverse is much harder.
- If you must rent out your time early, only do so while learning and saving, preferably in an apprenticeship-type field (chief of staff to a founder). Seek the steepest learning curve and take on accountability, which "you can take on immediately." Compensation follows once you've stopped waiting for it.
- Companies measure inputs because they can't measure outputs, so work in a way that makes your outputs visible. His investing school Spearhead found that generic classes were worth little, while office hours on specific deals were very valuable.
- On the long haul: "on a long enough timescale, you will get paid," but it can take 5 to 20 years. He says those he judged brilliant and hardworking two decades ago are almost all successful.
- Keep redefining what you do until you are the best in the world at it. Entrepreneurs only need to be right once.
- Wealth is not the final goal. "A fit body, a calm mind, a house full of love. These things cannot be bought, they must be earned."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Naval argues that once you have leverage (capital, people, code, media), your judgment determines outcomes. Judgment is built from experience, fast iteration and low emotion, and it earns trust through a public track record. Broad study, including philosophy, beats narrow domain reading.

chunks.heading: Leverage comes first, then judgment becomes the decisive skill
chunks.text:
- Naval says all great fortunes are created through leverage, and the first job is to obtain it.
- Permissioned leverage: getting people to work for you, or raising capital.
- Permissionless leverage: learning to code, or becoming a good communicator through podcasting, broadcasting, video and writing.
- The first part of a career is spent hustling to get leverage. Once you have it, he says to "slow down a bit, because your judgment really matters."
- His analogy: you go from steering a sailboat to steering an ocean liner or tanker. You have more at risk and more to gain, and you carry a higher payload.
- His conclusion: "In an age of infinite leverage, judgment becomes the most important skill." Leverage is a force multiplier for judgment.

chunks.heading: Why judgment is what the market pays for (Buffett and CEO pay)
chunks.text:
- Naval says everything else you do is setting you up to apply your judgment.
- Warren Buffett is wealthy because of his judgment. If you took all his money away, Naval says investors would "come out of the woodwork" and hand him $100 billion to invest, and he would keep a big chunk of it.
- On CEO pay: Naval grants that crony capitalism exists, with CEOs controlling boards. But some CEOs earn their keep.
- If you steer a $100 billion ship like Google or Apple and your judgment is 10 or 20 percent better than the next person's, society will pay you hundreds of millions more. Being on course more often compounds across hundreds of billions of dollars, so the pay is dwarfed by the results.
- Nobody asks Buffett how hard he works or when he wakes up. They say "Warren, just do your thing."

chunks.heading: Demonstrated judgment needs a public track record and accountability
chunks.text:
- Naval says demonstrated judgment and credibility are critical for getting people to put leverage behind you.
- Buffett wins because he has:
  - massive credibility
  - high accountability
  - been right over and over in the public domain
  - a reputation for very high integrity, so people can trust him
- Naval's formula: "Judgment, especially demonstrated judgment, with high accountability, clear track record, is critical."
- Nivi's summary, which Naval builds on: you are accountable for your judgment, judgment is the exercise of wisdom, and wisdom comes from experience that can be accelerated through short iterations.

chunks.heading: Defining judgment and wisdom
chunks.text:
- Judgment is knowing the long-term consequences of your actions, then making the right decision to capitalize on that.
- Naval's definition of wisdom is the same thing: knowing the long-term consequences of your actions.
- Wisdom is judgment applied to the personal domain. Judgment is wisdom applied to external problems. He calls them highly linked.

chunks.heading: Build judgment through experience and many fast iterations, not intellect alone
chunks.text:
- Judgment is very hard to build, and it takes both intellect and experience.
- Naval agrees with Nassim Taleb's criticism of ivory-tower intellectuals, who have no skin in the game and no real-world experience.
- Intellect without experience is "often worse than useless." It gives you confidence and some credibility, but with no skin in the game or accountability, "you're just throwing darts."
- The real world is far more complex than we can intellectualize. This is especially true of fast-moving edge domains, where you can't get there without experience.
- His tactic: if you are smart and iterate fast, it's "not even you put 10,000 hours into something, but you take 10,000 tries at something."

chunks.heading: The best judges are the least emotional
chunks.text:
- Naval says the people with the best judgment are among the least emotional. Many top investors seem almost robotic, and he wouldn't be surprised if the best entrepreneurs often come across as unemotional.
- Entrepreneurs have to care about what they're doing, but they also have to see clearly what is actually happening.
- Emotions are what stop you from seeing reality, in investing, running companies, building products or being an entrepreneur.
- The cost of this: you resist the truth until it becomes too sudden, and then you are forced into suffering as the fantasy you built breaks.
- His outrage test: the more outraged someone is, the worse their judgment. Someone constantly tweeting political outrage and getting into fights is not someone you would hand "the keys to your car, let alone the keys to your company."

chunks.heading: Study broadly, including philosophy, to build judgment
chunks.text:
- Naval notes that top value investors such as Warren Buffett, Jeremy Grantham and Michael Burry sound like philosophers, or are philosophers. They read a lot of history and science.
- He says investment books are "the worst place to learn about investment." Investing is a real-world, highly multivariate activity, and every advantage is always being competed away. It is always on the cutting edge.
- What you need instead is "very, very broad-based judgment and thinking," and the best way to get it is to study everything, including a lot of philosophy.
- Philosophy makes you more stoic and less emotional, so you make better decisions.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Naval explains that getting paid at scale requires accountability, leverage and specific knowledge, and that specific knowledge is the hardest to grasp. It can't be taught in a class, is found by following genuine curiosity and innate talent, feels like play to you but looks like work to others, and is often spotted first by people who know you well.

chunks.heading: Specific knowledge is the part of your pay that training cannot reproduce
chunks.text:
- Naval frames earning money as three pieces: getting paid at scale (leverage), being the one who gets paid (accountability), and being paid instead of somebody else (specific knowledge).
- He calls specific knowledge the hardest idea in his tweetstorm and the one people confuse most.
- His core claim: "everything can be learned," but not everything can be taught, and "the most interesting things cannot be taught."
- Specific knowledge tends to come from one of four places:
  - Innate traits in your DNA.
  - Childhood soft skills that are very hard to teach later.
  - Brand new fields where nobody else knows how yet.
  - On-the-job training that builds judgment by pattern matching in complex environments.
- His examples of domain judgment: investing, running a fleet of trucks, weather forecasting.

chunks.heading: Why anything you can be trained for pays only minimum wage
chunks.text:
- If a class can teach the skill, others can be trained too, and then people can be mass-produced, programmed into computers, and eventually into robots.
- Naval's conclusion: a trainable person is "extremely replaceable," so the pay falls to the minimum needed to attract the many other people who could be trained.
- Returns on trainable skills "devolve into your cost of training plus the return on investment on that training."
- Training and schooling still matter, because you need them to capitalize on specific knowledge. But the part the market pays you for is the specific knowledge, not the training.

chunks.heading: Find specific knowledge through curiosity and talent, not hot fields
chunks.text:
- Specific knowledge comes from your innate talents, genuine curiosity and passion. It does not come from "going to school for whatever is the hottest job" or entering whatever field investors say is hottest.
- Example: a psychology degree is leverage for someone who is already a formidable salesperson. For a lifelong introvert who was never good at sales, psychology will not make them great at it.
- It often sits at the edge of knowledge, in things just being figured out or very hard to figure out.
- After roughly age 20 to 22, he says you almost don't get to choose your specific knowledge. You look at what you have already built and build on top of it.

chunks.heading: Why you must be 100% into it: leverage and compounding punish the second best
chunks.text:
- "If you're not 100% into it somebody else who is 100% into it will outperform you," and not by a little, because ideas are a domain where compound interest and leverage apply.
- His numeric illustration: at 1,000 times leverage, someone right 90% of the time versus someone right 80% of the time gets paid "hundreds of times more by the market."
- This is why genuine curiosity matters so much. It is what gets you to be correct more often than everyone else in the field.

chunks.heading: Your specific knowledge feels like play to you and looks like work to others
chunks.text:
- Specific knowledge is usually found by observation, not reasoning. You look back on your own life and see what you are actually good at.
- Naval's own case: he wanted to be a scientist and built his value system around scientists, whom he sees as the top of the production chain for humanity. But what he was uniquely good at was making money, tinkering with technology, and selling and explaining ideas.
- His specific skills, in his words:

chunks.heading: Other people often spot your specific knowledge before you do
chunks.text:
- Naval's mother identified his real specific knowledge at about 15 or 16. When he said he would be an astrophysicist, she said from the kitchen, "No, you're going to go into business."
- She had seen him critique local pizza parlors as they walked down the street: why they sold slices a certain way, with certain toppings, and why the ordering process should be different.
- That business-curious mind combined with his obsession with science and led him to technology businesses.
- His takeaway: your specific knowledge is "observed and often observed by other people who know you well and revealed in situations rather than something that you come up with."
